page.mentor_intro: Stress ulcer prophylaxis (SUP) in the intensive care unit is aimed at preventing stress-related mucosal bleeding in critically ill patients. Routine universal prophylaxis is no longer supported; targeted therapy balances gastroprotection against the risks of hospital-acquired pneumonia and Clostridioides difficile infection.

teaching_points.claim: Stress-related mucosal disease (SRMD) develops from splanchnic hypoperfusion, mucosal ischemia, and impaired bicarbonate secretion in critically ill patients; clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding carries high attributable mortality, but occurs in <2–3% of modern ICU patients.

Independent risk factors mandating stress ulcer prophylaxis include: mechanical ventilation anticipated for >48 hours and severe coagulopathy (platelet count <50,000/uL, INR >1.5, or PTT >2 times control).

The landmark PEPTIC trial (over 26,000 ICU patients) and the SUP-ICU trial demonstrated that Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs, e.g., pantoprazole 40 mg daily) and Histamine-2 Receptor Antagonists (H2RAs, e.g., famotidine 20 mg twice daily) achieve low rates of overt GI bleeding without significant differences in 90-day all-cause mortality.

Acid suppression alters upper gastrointestinal and pulmonary microflora: chronic PPI therapy in the ICU is associated with a modest but statistically significant increased risk of hospital-acquired pneumonia and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea.

Prophylaxis should be discontinued promptly once major risk factors resolve (extubation from mechanical ventilation, resolution of shock and coagulopathy, and establishment of full enteral nutrition) to prevent inappropriate outpatient continuation.

uncertainties: Impact of high-dose early enteral nutrition alone as protective against stress mucosal bleeding without concurrent pharmacological acid suppression.
Optimal comparative choice between intravenous H2RAs versus PPIs in neurocritical intensive care patients with traumatic brain injury.
mcq_angles: Mandatory indications for stress ulcer prophylaxis: invasive mechanical ventilation >48 hours and clinically significant coagulopathy (platelets <50k or INR >1.5).
PEPTIC trial finding: PPIs and H2RAs demonstrate equivalent 90-day mortality and low rates of clinically significant GI bleeding in mechanical ventilation.
Adverse effect trade-off of acid suppression: increased risks of Clostridioides difficile colitis and ventilator-associated pneumonia secondary to loss of gastric acid barrier.
case_hooks: A 64-year-old mechanically ventilated man with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome on day 4 of ICU admission with normal platelets and coagulation, evaluated for SUP.
A 72-year-old woman recovering from septic shock extubated on day 5 and tolerating full enteral nutrition, whose pantoprazole is discontinued upon ICU stepdown.

page.mentor_intro: Evidence-based prescribing of stress ulcer prophylaxis requires identifying specific high-risk critical care cohorts while avoiding overuse in low-risk ward and ICU populations. Re-evaluating daily indications minimizes drug-drug interactions and infectious sequelae.

teaching_points.claim: Primary high-risk indications for SUP encompass: invasive mechanical ventilation >=48 hours, severe coagulopathy (INR >1.5, platelets <50 x 10^9/L), traumatic brain injury (GCS <=8), major severe burn injury (>35% BSA), and polytrauma with high injury severity score.

Secondary lower-risk contributing factors that may justify prophylaxis when multiple are present include: septic shock requiring vasopressors, acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy, high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy (>250 mg hydrocortisone equivalent daily), and a documented history of GI ulceration within the past year.

In patients receiving full enteral nutrition, nutritional infusion provides direct luminal buffering and mucosal blood flow promotion; randomized trials indicate that enteral nutrition alone significantly attenuates stress ulceration risk.

Proton pump inhibitors provide more potent acid suppression than H2-receptor antagonists and avoid the tachyphylaxis (tolerance within 48 to 72 hours) characteristic of H2RAs; however, both drug classes have comparable clinical outcomes in large pragmatic trials.

Failure to discontinue stress ulcer prophylaxis upon discharge from the ICU results in inappropriate long-term outpatient acid suppression in up to 50–70% of survivors, predisposing patients to bone fractures, hypomagnesemia, and recurrent enteric infections.

uncertainties: Biomarkers or gastric mucosal pH monitoring in predicting overt stress-induced mucosal ulceration before clinical bleeding occurs.
Comparative cost-effectiveness of oral sucralfate mucosal coating versus systemic acid-suppressive agents in modern critical care.
mcq_angles: Tachyphylaxis with H2-receptor antagonists: rapid tolerance develops within 48 to 72 hours of continuous H2RA infusion, whereas PPIs maintain consistent acid suppression.
Discontinuation trigger: extubation and establishment of enteral nutrition should trigger immediate cessation of stress ulcer prophylaxis in the absence of other risk factors.
Risk of outpatient discharge continuation: inappropriate post-discharge continuation of inpatient acid suppression exposes patients to long-term chronic kidney disease and micronutrient deficiencies.

page.mentor_intro: Acute stroke is a devastating syndrome of rapidly developing clinical signs of focal or global disturbance of cerebral function lasting >24 hours or leading to death, with no apparent cause other than vascular origin. It is divided into acute ischaemic stroke (85%, caused by large vessel thrombosis, embolic occlusion, or microvascular lacunar disease) and haemorrhagic stroke (15%, comprising spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage). Emergency management hinges on time-critical neuroimaging ('time is brain') to rule out haemorrhage, determine ischemic core vs salvageable penumbra, and immediately deploy reperfusion therapies (intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and mechanical thrombectomy within 6 to 24 hours).

teaching_points.claim: Emergency non-contrast head CT or brain MRI is the mandatory initial imaging investigation in suspected acute stroke to definitively differentiate ischaemic stroke from acute intracerebral haemorrhage.

Intravenous thrombolysis with tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) or alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) is indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients without contraindications (e.g., active bleeding, severe hypertension >185/110 mmHg, recent surgery, therapeutic anticoagulation).

Endovascular mechanical thrombectomy (EVT) is the gold standard standard of care for acute ischaemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion (LVO) of the anterior circulation (internal carotid artery or proximal MCA-M1), demonstrating profound disability reduction when performed within 6 hours, and up to 24 hours in selected patients with perfusion mismatch (DAWN and DEFUSE-3 trials).

In acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH), immediate blood pressure lowering to a systolic target of 130-140 mmHg within 2 hours is safe and attenuates hematoma expansion (INTERACT-2 and ATACH-2 trials), alongside immediate reversal of any anticoagulant agents.

uncertainties: Benefit of mechanical thrombectomy in patients presenting with large ischemic core volume (ASPECTS 3-5) on acute baseline imaging.
Optimal blood pressure targets during and immediately following successful endovascular recanalization in acute ischaemic stroke.
mcq_angles: Blood pressure thresholds for thrombolysis: blood pressure must be lowered below 185/110 mmHg prior to administering IV alteplase/tenecteplase, and maintained <180/105 mmHg for the first 24 hours post-thrombolysis.
Endovascular thrombectomy time windows: standard 0-6 hours vs extended 6-24 hour window guided by CT perfusion (ischemic core vs penumbra volume).

Anticoagulation reversal protocols in acute haemorrhagic stroke (4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate [4F-PCC] plus vitamin K for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for factor Xa inhibitors).
case_hooks: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the ED 75 minutes after sudden onset of right dense hemiplegia and severe global aphasia (NIHSS 18); non-contrast head CT is normal (ASPECTS 10) and CT angiogram reveals a left MCA M1 occlusion.

A 72-year-old male on apixaban for atrial fibrillation collapses with sudden severe headache, vomiting, and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9; CT demonstrates a 45 mL acute intracerebral haematoma in the right basal ganglia.

page.mentor_intro: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most frequent sustained cardiac arrhythmia, conferring a 5-fold increased risk of cardioembolic ischaemic stroke and systemic thromboembolism. Cardioembolic strokes originating from left atrial appendage thrombi in AF are characterized by greater severity, larger infarct size, higher recurrence, and higher mortality compared to other stroke subtypes. Thromboembolic risk stratification using the CHA2DS2-VASc score guides anticoagulation: direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) represent the first-line therapy over warfarin, while percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) serves as an alternative for patients with absolute long-term contraindications.

teaching_points.claim: Oral anticoagulation is strongly recommended for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF in men with a CHA2DS2-VASc score >=2 and women with >=3, and should be considered in men with score = 1 and women with score = 2.

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) are superior to warfarin, exhibiting equivalent or superior thromboembolic reduction with a ~50% reduction in catastrophic intracranial haemorrhage and lower all-cause mortality.

Aspirin or antiplatelet monotherapy is ineffective for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation and carries bleeding risks comparable to oral anticoagulants; antiplatelet monotherapy is strictly not recommended for stroke prophylaxis in AF guidelines.

Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC, e.g., Watchman, Amulet devices) is an evidence-based non-pharmacologic alternative for patients with non-valvular AF at high stroke risk who have absolute, non-modifiable contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation.

uncertainties: Role of oral anticoagulation in patients with subclinical, device-detected atrial high-rate episodes (AHREs / silent AF lasting <24 hours) detected on pacemakers or wearables (ARTESiA and NOAH-AFNET 4 trials).
Comparative long-term ischemic and bleeding outcomes of next-generation left atrial appendage occlusion devices versus modern DOAC monotherapy.
mcq_angles: Calculating the CHA2DS2-VASc score and identifying treatment thresholds where oral anticoagulation is definitively indicated.
Explaining the fundamental advantage of DOACs over warfarin (specifically the dramatic 50% relative risk reduction in fatal intracranial haemorrhage).
Inappropriateness of aspirin or clopidogrel for stroke prevention in AF (lack of stroke efficacy with bleeding risk near anticoagulation).
case_hooks: A 69-year-old male with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and newly diagnosed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc = 3) presents to clinic; he asks if he can take baby aspirin instead of a blood thinner.

A 76-year-old female with persistent AF and a history of recurrent severe angiodysplastic lower GI bleeding requiring frequent transfusions is evaluated for percutaneous left atrial appendage closure.

page.mentor_intro: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency. After securing the aneurysm, nimodipine reduces poor outcome, delayed cerebral ischaemia is watched for between days 4 and 14, and triple-H therapy is no longer used.

teaching_points.claim: Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days improves outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage; its benefit is not due to preventing angiographic vasospasm.
Delayed cerebral ischaemia typically occurs between days 4 and 14 and is monitored by neurological examination with transcranial Doppler or CT angiography/perfusion.
Treatment of delayed ischaemia aims for euvolaemia and induced hypertension if needed; routine hypervolaemia and haemodilution (triple-H therapy) are no longer recommended.
The aneurysm is secured early, by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping; ISAT favoured coiling for suitable aneurysms.

Why triple-H therapy was abandoned.

page.mentor_intro: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is a neurological catastrophe characterized by high initial mortality and complex delayed secondary cerebral complications. Intensive care management centers on emergent aneurysm securing, neuroprotective nimodipine, aggressive vasospasm surveillance, and maintenance of euvolemia.

teaching_points.claim: Immediate emergency priority in aneurysmal SAH is early securing of the ruptured aneurysm (within 24 to 48 hours) via endovascular coiling or microsurgical clipping to prevent fatal rebleeding (rebleeding risk is highest in the first 24 hours, carrying >50% mortality); endovascular coiling is favored in anatomically suitable anterior circulation aneurysms (ISAT trial).

Oral nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours for exactly 21 days) is the only pharmacological neuroprotective agent proven in randomized clinical trials to improve neurological outcomes and reduce delayed ischemic deficits, acting through cellular neuroprotective mechanisms rather than gross cerebral arterial vasodilation.

Delayed Cerebral Ischemia (DCI)—secondary to microvascular dysfunction, cortical spreading depolarization, microthrombosis, and macrovascular arterial vasospasm—classically develops between days 4 and 14 post-hemorrhage; monitoring incorporates daily transcranial Doppler (TCD: mean flow velocity >120-200 cm/s in MCA indicates vasospasm) and serial neurological examinations.

Management of delayed cerebral ischemia requires induced hypertension (elevating MAP using noradrenaline targeting SBP 160–180 mmHg or 20–30 mmHg above baseline in secured aneurysms) and maintenance of strict euvolemia; legacy 'Triple-H' therapy (Hypervolemia, Hemodilution, Hypertension) has been abandoned due to risks of pulmonary edema and myocardial infarction without clinical benefit.

Hyponatremia occurs in >30–50% of SAH patients, predominantly driven by Cerebral Salt Wasting (CSW, hypovolemic hyponatremia with high urine sodium) or SIADH (euvolemic hyponatremia); CSW must be treated with volume and sodium repletion (hypertonic saline 3% or fludrocortisone), avoiding fluid restriction which precipitates cerebral infarction.

uncertainties: Role of continuous intra-arterial vasodilator infusions (milrinone, nicardipine) versus balloon angioplasty in refractory proximal delayed cerebral vasospasm.
Prognostic utility of continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) in detecting non-convulsive seizures and cortical spreading depolarizations in comatose SAH patients.
mcq_angles: Nimodipine protocol in aSAH: oral nimodipine (60 mg q4h for 21 days) is mandatory; IV formulation increases hypotension and does not improve outcomes over oral delivery.
Management of hyponatremia in SAH: fluid restriction is strictly contraindicated; differentiate CSW from SIADH and maintain euvolemia/hypervolemia with isotonic or hypertonic saline.
Modern hemodynamic strategy for DCI: induced hypertension with euvolemia (monitored by noradrenaline titration); hypervolemia and hemodilution are abandoned.
case_hooks: A 52-year-old woman presenting with a 'thunderclap' headache, Hunt and Hess Grade 2 aSAH, whose basilar tip aneurysm is successfully coiled within 18 hours.
A 48-year-old woman on day 7 post-SAH who develops new-onset expressive dysphasia and right pronator drift with MCA flow velocity 210 cm/s on TCD.

page.mentor_intro: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a biochemical diagnosis defined by an elevated serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level with normal circulating free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3). Deciding when to initiate levothyroxine therapy balances cardiovascular and symptom benefits against the risks of overtreatment, guided by TSH cutoffs and patient age.

teaching_points.claim: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined biochemically by a confirmed elevated serum TSH (above the reference range, typically >4.0–4.5 mIU/L) with normal circulating free T4 (FT4); repeat testing at 2 to 3 months is mandatory before diagnosis, as up to 50% of mildly elevated TSH values spontaneously normalize.

A serum TSH threshold >=10.0 mIU/L represents an established consensus indication for levothyroxine replacement therapy across all age groups, based on observational evidence showing increased risks of heart failure, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and progression to overt hypothyroidism (~5% per year).

For mild TSH elevations (4.5 to 9.9 mIU/L), routine treatment is NOT recommended in adults aged >=65–70 years (TRUST trial), as levothyroxine does not improve quality of life, fatigue, or cognitive function in older adults and increases the risk of iatrogenic atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis.

Indications for treating mild TSH elevation (4.5 to 9.9 mIU/L) in younger adults (<65 years) include: persistent symptoms of hypothyroidism, positive anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, presence of a goiter, or planning pregnancy.

In pregnancy or women actively pursuing conception, treatment thresholds are significantly more aggressive: levothyroxine is recommended if TSH is above the pregnancy-specific upper limit (>4.0 mIU/L) or >2.5 mIU/L in the presence of positive anti-TPO antibodies, to prevent miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, and neurodevelopmental impairment.

uncertainties: Cardiovascular risk reduction magnitude of levothyroxine in young adults (age 35-55) with mild subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 7.0-9.9 mIU/L).
Optimal long-term monitoring intervals for untreated older patients maintaining stable TSH levels between 5.0 and 8.0 mIU/L.
mcq_angles: TRUST trial landmark finding in older adults: levothyroxine replacement in adults >=65 years with subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4.5-9.9) provides NO benefit for hypothyroid symptoms or fatigue.
Definitive TSH treatment threshold: TSH >=10.0 mIU/L warrants levothyroxine therapy regardless of age due to increased cardiovascular mortality and risk of heart failure.
Pregnancy-specific threshold: levothyroxine is indicated if TSH >2.5 mIU/L with positive anti-TPO antibodies or TSH >4.0 mIU/L irrespective of antibody status.

page.mentor_intro: Substance use disorder (SUD) is a chronic, relapsing brain disease characterized by compulsive drug seeking and use despite devastating personal, social, and physical consequences. SUD spans multiple substance classes—opioids, alcohol, cannabis, sedatives/hypnotics, stimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine), and tobacco—diagnosed by DSM-5 criteria across impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological criteria (tolerance and withdrawal). Effective management integrates evidence-based harm reduction (naloxone distribution, needle exchange), maintenance agonist pharmacotherapies for opioid and alcohol disorders, and structured behavioural therapies.

teaching_points.claim: Opioid use disorder (OUD) maintenance therapy with opioid agonists (buprenorphine-naloxone or methadone) represents the gold standard of care, significantly reducing illicit opioid use, criminal activity, transmission of HIV/HCV, and all-cause and overdose mortality.

Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid receptor agonist with high binding affinity; initiating buprenorphine too early before the onset of objective opioid withdrawal (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale [COWS] >=8-12) will displace full agonists and precipitate severe withdrawal.
Harm reduction strategies, prominently wide community distribution of intranasal naloxone, provide life-saving emergency reversal of opioid overdose without increasing substance consumption.

For alcohol use disorder, FDA-approved pharmacotherapies—acamprosate (modulating glutamate/GABA neurotransmission) and naltrexone (mu-opioid receptor antagonist reducing alcohol craving and heavy drinking days)—are underutilized first-line medical options.

uncertainties: Optimal induction strategies for buprenorphine in the era of high-potency synthetic fentanyl analogs with prolonged lipophilic terminal elimination.
Efficacy of sub-dissociative ketamine infusions or psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy in sustaining abstinence in treatment-resistant substance use disorders.
mcq_angles: Mechanisms and prevention of precipitated withdrawal during buprenorphine induction (utilizing COWS scoring or micro-dosing / Bernese method).
Selecting acamprosate over naltrexone in alcohol use disorder in patients with significant hepatic transaminitis or concurrent opioid use.
Emergency administration and repeat dosing of naloxone in synthetic opioid (fentanyl) overdoses due to high potency and receptor displacement requirements.
case_hooks: A 27-year-old male with severe opioid use disorder presents requesting buprenorphine-naloxone; he injected heroin 4 hours ago, has a COWS score of 3, and asks for his first sublingual dose immediately.
A 45-year-old executive with severe alcohol use disorder achieving supervised detoxification wishes to start medication to reduce intense alcohol cravings; AST is 185 U/L and ALT is 142 U/L.

page.mentor_intro: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is an otolaryngological emergency characterized by rapid-onset sensorineural hearing impairment developing within 72 hours. Immediate clinical diagnosis and urgent initiation of high-dose corticosteroids within the initial therapeutic window dictate recovery.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnostic criteria for SSNHL require sensorineural hearing loss of >=30 decibels (dB) affecting at least three contiguous audiometric frequencies, developing over a period of <=72 hours; it is predominantly unilateral (98%) and idiopathic in >90% of cases.

Emergency bedside tuning fork assessment: Weber test lateralizes to the UNAFFECTED normal ear (indicating sensorineural loss in the affected ear), and Rinne test demonstrates air conduction greater than bone conduction (AC > BC, positive Rinne) bilaterally, ruling out conductive cerumen impaction or middle ear effusion.

High-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy is the mainstay of treatment, initiated as early as possible within 2 weeks of symptom onset: oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, typically 60 mg daily for 7 to 14 days followed by a taper) promotes resolution by reducing cochlear edema and microvascular inflammation.

Intratympanic (IT) corticosteroid injections (dexamethasone or methylprednisolone injected through the tympanic membrane into the middle ear) achieve high perilymph concentrations without systemic side effects; IT steroids are recommended as salvage therapy for incomplete recovery after systemic steroids or as primary therapy in patients with contraindications to systemic steroids (uncontrolled diabetes, severe hypertension).

Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and internal auditory canals (IACs) is mandatory in all patients with confirmed SSNHL to rule out a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma, found in 2–5% of SSNHL cases), stroke, or demyelinating disease.

uncertainties: Additive therapeutic benefit of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) combined with corticosteroids versus corticosteroids alone in severe profound SSNHL.
Prognostic significance of initial audiogram configuration (upsloping low-frequency loss carrying superior recovery vs flat/downsloping profound loss).
mcq_angles: Tuning fork findings in unilateral sensorineural hearing loss: Weber test lateralizes to the normal opposite ear; Rinne test is positive (AC > BC) in both ears.
Therapeutic window for corticosteroids: maximal recovery occurs when systemic corticosteroids are initiated within 72 hours to 14 days of symptom onset; efficacy declines sharply after 2–4 weeks.
Mandatory imaging modality: contrast-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals is required to rule out vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).

page.mentor_intro: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP) is the leading cause of epilepsy-related mortality, defined as the non-traumatic, non-drowning sudden death of an individual with epilepsy with or without evidence of a seizure. Transparent patient counseling, optimizing seizure control, and nocturnal supervision are life-saving.

teaching_points.claim: SUDEP is defined as a sudden, unexpected, witnessed or unwitnessed, non-traumatic, and non-drowning death in a patient with epilepsy, with or without evidence of an antecedent seizure, where post-mortem examination does not reveal a toxicological or anatomical cause of death.

The single greatest modifiable risk factor for SUDEP is the frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS): patients experiencing >=3 GTCS per year have a >15-fold increased risk of SUDEP compared to seizure-free individuals.

Major secondary risk factors include: nocturnal seizures, sleeping alone/unsupervised, prone sleeping position ('face-down' post-ictal suffocation), early age of epilepsy onset, long disease duration, and poor adherence to antiseizure medications (ASMs).

The proposed terminal pathophysiological mechanism (MORTEMUS study) involves a post-ictal sequence: a generalized convulsive seizure triggers post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES), followed by central hypopnea/apnea, bradyarrhythmia or asystole, and secondary terminal cardiac arrest.

Counseling and preventive strategies: transparent counseling regarding SUDEP is recommended by guidelines (NICE, AAN); the primary prevention is maximizing seizure control to abolish GTCS, promoting medication adherence, avoiding sleep deprivation and excess alcohol, utilizing nocturnal supervision/monitors, and avoiding prone sleep posturing.

uncertainties: Clinical efficacy of wearable smartwatch/accelerometer seizure detection devices in reducing true SUDEP incidence through prompt caregiver alerting.
Role of adjunctive selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) in mitigating post-ictal respiratory depression and central apnea.
mcq_angles: Single strongest modifiable risk factor for SUDEP: frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS); complete control of GTCS dramatically reduces SUDEP risk.
Post-ictal sleep position hazard: prone sleeping position is found in >70% of unwitnessed SUDEP cases, contributing to post-ictal suffocation and respiratory arrest.
Guideline communication standard: clinicians should discuss SUDEP early with patients and families to emphasize the critical importance of antiseizure medication adherence.

page.mentor_intro: Suicide risk assessment is a mandatory core clinical competency across all medical, psychiatric, and emergency specialties. Suicide risk formulation has evolved from crude, inaccurate categorical risk categorization ('low, medium, high') to personalized, dynamic, collaborative risk formulation and safety planning. Key clinical components include distinguishing suicidal ideation from intent and plan, evaluating accessible lethal means, identifying modifiable risk factors (major depression, bipolar disorder, substance misuse, severe agitation), and recognizing evidence-based anti-suicidal pharmacotherapies (lithium, clozapine).

teaching_points.claim: Asking directly and empathetically about suicidal thoughts, intent, and plans does NOT induce or increase suicidal ideation or behaviour; rather, it reduces distress and opens essential therapeutic dialogue.

Categorical risk prediction tools and rating scales cannot accurately predict individual suicidal behaviour and should never be used in isolation to determine hospital admission or discharge decisions.

Lethal means restriction—specifically securing firearms, safe disposal of toxic medications, and bridge barriers—is the single most effective public health and clinical intervention for reducing suicide deaths.

Lithium in bipolar disorder and major depression, and clozapine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia spectrum disorders, are the only psychotropic medications with robust randomized evidence demonstrating specific long-term reduction in suicide and suicide attempts.

uncertainties: Short-term versus long-term anti-suicidal efficacy of rapid-acting interventions such as intravenous ketamine and intranasal esketamine in acute emergency department presentations.
Reliability and ethical governance of artificial intelligence and electronic health record predictive algorithms for automated suicide risk detection.
mcq_angles: Evidence-based anti-suicidal properties of lithium in mood disorders and clozapine in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
The role of the Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention (collaborative personalized coping strategies and emergency contacts) over ineffective 'no-suicide contracts'.
Emergency psychiatric evaluation: identifying imminent warning signs (active preparatory acts, explicit suicide notes, saying goodbyes, sudden calm after severe depression).

page.mentor_intro: Suicide risk assessment requires an empathic, structured clinical interview to evaluate intent, identify psychiatric and situational risk factors, and co-design a personalized safety plan. Moving beyond simplistic risk stratification checklists improves clinical engagement and patient safety.

teaching_points.claim: Evidence-based guidelines (NICE, APA) explicitly advise against utilizing actuarial or numerical risk categorization tools (e.g., categorizing patients into 'low', 'medium', or 'high' risk) to guide clinical management, as these tools have unacceptable false-negative rates and fail to predict completed suicide.

A comprehensive clinical risk formulation systematically evaluates: suicidal ideation (frequency, intensity, duration), specific plan and lethal feasibility, preparatory behaviors (acquiring means, writing notes, giving away belongings), and degree of suicidal intent versus ambivalence.

Self-harm (non-suicidal self-injury [NSSI] vs suicide attempts) must be differentiated: NSSI is typically performed to regulate overwhelming negative affect, alleviate distress, or express emotional pain without intent to die; however, chronic NSSI is a powerful independent longitudinal risk factor for future suicide attempts.

The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) is an evidence-based clinical tool comprising six sequential steps: identifying personalized warning signs, internal coping strategies, social contacts/distractions, trusted family/friends for support, professional crisis services, and making the environment safe (restricting access to lethal means).

Pharmacological interventions with proven, specific antisuicidal properties include: Lithium in bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder (reduces suicide attempts and completed suicides by >60%), Clozapine in schizophrenia (the only FDA-approved antipsychotic for reducing suicidal behavior), and rapid-acting subanesthetic ketamine/esketamine for acute depressive crises.

uncertainties: Long-term real-world effectiveness of digital smartphone safety-planning applications versus physical paper-based safety plans in reducing crisis readmissions.
Clinical thresholds for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) in acute suicidal crises with psychotic depression.
mcq_angles: Psychiatric medication with proven antisuicidal properties in mood disorders: Lithium significantly reduces completed suicide rates independent of its antidepressant maintenance efficacy.
Clozapine unique regulatory indication: the only antipsychotic with a specific FDA indication for reducing suicidal behavior in schizophrenia.
Guideline consensus on risk scales: numeric risk stratification scales should not be used to determine admission or discharge; clinical risk formulation and safety planning are required.
case_hooks: A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder presenting to the emergency department after superficial forearm cutting following abandonment by her partner.

page.mentor_intro: Superficial vein thrombosis (SVT / superficial thrombophlebitis) was historically considered a benign localized condition, but is now recognized as part of the venous thromboembolism (VTE) spectrum. Accurately distinguishing SVT from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and evaluating for concurrent deep propagation is essential.

teaching_points.claim: Superficial vein thrombosis (SVT) presents with localized pain, erythema, tenderness, and a palpable, tender, indurated subcutaneous 'cord' along the anatomical course of a superficial vein (most commonly the great saphenous vein [GSV]); deep vein thrombosis (DVT) typically presents with diffuse unilateral calf or whole-leg swelling, edema, and calf tenderness without a visible superficial cord.

Comprehensive duplex venous ultrasonography of the entire lower extremity is mandatory in all patients with suspected SVT to measure the exact thrombus length and rule out concurrent deep vein thrombosis, which is present in 20–25% of patients presenting with apparent isolated SVT.

In patients with isolated lower extremity SVT that is >=5 cm in length and located >=3 cm from the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) or saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ), the landmark CALISTO randomized trial established that subcutaneous fondaparinux (2.5 mg once daily for 45 days) significantly reduces the composite of death, PE, DVT, or SVT extension by 85% without increasing major bleeding.

SVT extending within 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction or saphenopopliteal junction carries high risk of embolization and is classified as equivalent to deep vein thrombosis, mandating full-dose therapeutic anticoagulation (DOACs or therapeutic LMWH) for at least 3 months.

Migratory or recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis in atypical sites without varicose veins (Trousseau syndrome) is a classic paraneoplastic manifestation of occult visceral adenocarcinoma (pancreatic, gastric, lung, or ovarian malignancy) or underlying systemic vasculitis (Behcet disease, Buerger disease).

uncertainties: Efficacy and safety of direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) compared to fondaparinux in isolated lower limb SVT (SURPRISE trial extrapolation).
Indications for thrombophilia screening in young patients presenting with unprovoked, recurrent superficial vein thrombosis.
mcq_angles: CALISTO trial regimen for extensive SVT: prophylactic-dose fondaparinux (2.5 mg daily for 45 days) is the evidence-based treatment for isolated SVT >=5 cm in length.
SVT within 3 cm of saphenofemoral junction: treated as deep vein thrombosis with full-dose therapeutic anticoagulation for 3 months due to high risk of progression into the common femoral vein.
Trousseau syndrome clinical significance: recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis is a paraneoplastic marker indicating underlying visceral adenocarcinoma (especially pancreatic cancer).
case_hooks: A 54-year-old woman presenting with a painful, erythematous, palpable 8-cm cord over the medial lower calf with duplex ultrasound confirming great saphenous vein SVT ending 12 cm below the SFJ.
A 62-year-old man presenting with acute groin tenderness whose duplex scan reveals great saphenous vein thrombosis extending to within 1.5 cm of the common femoral vein.

page.mentor_intro: Surgical site infections (SSIs) represent the most frequent healthcare-associated infection among surgical patients, contributing to prolonged hospitalization, readmission, sepsis, and substantial mortality. Prevention requires meticulous adherence to an evidence-based perioperative care bundle encompassing preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative interventions. Core components include timely weight-adjusted prophylactic antibiotics administered within 60 minutes prior to incision, alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, normothermia maintenance, intraoperative oxygenation, and tight glycaemic control.

teaching_points.claim: Preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis must be completely infused within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision (120 minutes for vancomycin or fluoroquinolones) to achieve bactericidal tissue levels during incision, and re-dosed intraoperatively if procedure duration exceeds two half-lives of the antibiotic.

Preoperative hair removal, if necessary, must be performed immediately prior to surgery using electric clippers; routine manual razors with blades are strictly contraindicated as they cause microscopic skin abrasions that harbor bacteria and dramatically increase SSI rates.
Alcoholic chlorhexidine gluconate skin preparation is significantly superior to aqueous povidone-iodine in reducing surgical site infections in clean-contaminated and clean procedures.

Prophylactic antibiotic administration should NOT be continued postoperatively beyond wound closure for uncomplicated clean and clean-contaminated procedures; continuing antibiotics for 24-48 hours post-op provides zero SSI reduction while driving Clostridioides difficile colitis and antibiotic resistance.

uncertainties: Efficacy and safety of intrawound vancomycin powder application in reducing deep periprosthetic and spinal surgical site infections.
Value of routine closed-incision negative pressure wound therapy (ciNPWT) over conventional sterile dressings in high-risk abdominal wounds.
mcq_angles: Optimal timing of preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis (within 60 minutes prior to incision) and intraoperative re-dosing intervals (e.g., cefazolin re-dosed at 4 hours).
Hair removal techniques: electric clippers over razors to prevent microabrasions and SSI.
Evidence-based cessation of prophylactic antibiotics at wound closure versus inappropriate routine 24-hour postoperative continuation.
case_hooks: A 62-year-old obese diabetic male is scheduled for elective sigmoid resection for diverticular disease; the surgical trainee plans preoperative skin preparation and timing of prophylactic IV cefazolin plus metronidazole.

page.mentor_intro: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are the most common healthcare-associated infections among surgical patients, contributing to prolonged hospitalization, readmission, and morbidity. Implementing evidence-based preventive care bundles across preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative phases significantly reduces infection rates.

teaching_points.claim: CDC classifications divide SSIs into: (1) Superficial incisional (involves only skin and subcutaneous tissue within 30 days), (2) Deep incisional (involves deep soft tissues, fascial and muscle layers within 30 to 90 days), and (3) Organ/Space (involves any anatomical part opened or manipulated during surgery within 30 to 90 days).

Preoperative hair removal: routine shaving with razors causes microscopic skin abrasions that harbor bacteria and significantly increases SSI rates; if hair removal is necessary, electric clippers with a single-use blade immediately prior to surgery must be used.

Surgical skin antisepsis: chlorhexidine gluconate in an alcoholic solution (2% chlorhexidine in 70% isopropyl alcohol) is guideline-preferred (WHO, CDC, NICE) over povidone-iodine due to superior residual bactericidal persistence and lower SSI incidence in clean-contaminated surgeries.

Intraoperative physiological optimization requires: maintaining strict normothermia (core temperature >=36.0 C via active forced-air warming blankets, preventing hypothermia-induced vasoconstriction and impaired neutrophil killing), perioperative glycemic control (blood glucose <200 mg/dL / <11 mmol/L in all patients), and maintaining adequate tissue oxygenation via normovolemia.

Management of established incisional SSI requires: opening the surgical incision to evacuate purulent collections, debriding devitalized tissue, taking deep tissue specimens for Gram stain and culture, and packing with saline-moistened sterile gauze or applying negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT); systemic antibiotics are indicated only if systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia) or surrounding erythema >5 cm is present.

uncertainties: Clinical efficacy of prophylactic closed incisional negative pressure wound therapy (ciNPWT) in clean-contaminated high-risk abdominal incisions.
Comparative effectiveness of supplemental high fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2 80% vs 30-35%) in reducing SSI rates in mechanically ventilated surgical patients.
mcq_angles: Hair removal standard of care: hair should NOT be removed routinely; if required, electric clipping immediately before surgery is mandatory; razors are strictly contraindicated.
Skin preparation agent of choice: alcoholic chlorhexidine gluconate is superior to aqueous povidone-iodine in preventing surgical site infections.
Hypothermia prevention mechanism: maintaining core normothermia (>=36 C) prevents peripheral vasoconstriction and preserves neutrophil oxidative bactericidal burst.

page.mentor_intro: Antimicrobial surgical prophylaxis is a time-critical intervention designed to achieve bactericidal tissue concentrations at the precise moment of incision. Adherence to strict administration windows, redosing intervals, and targeted MRSA screening prevents SSI without fostering antimicrobial resistance.

teaching_points.claim: Timing of surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis: intravenous antibiotics must be completely infused within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision (or within 120 minutes for agents with long infusion times like vancomycin or fluoroquinolones) to guarantee peak tissue drug concentrations at the moment of initial skin incision.

Postoperative discontinuation: antimicrobial prophylaxis should be discontinued within 24 hours of surgery completion (or immediately at wound closure); continuing prophylactic antibiotics postoperatively does NOT reduce SSI rates and promotes Clostridioides difficile colitis and multidrug-resistant pathogen emergence.

Intraoperative redosing is mandatory if the procedure duration exceeds two half-lives of the antibiotic (e.g., redose cefazolin every 3 to 4 hours) or in cases of massive intraoperative blood loss (>1,500 mL) to maintain adequate minimum inhibitory concentrations.

Cefazolin (2 g IV for patients <120 kg, or 3 g IV for patients >=120 kg) is the standard workhorse prophylactic agent for clean and clean-contaminated procedures; broad-spectrum agents with anaerobic coverage (cefazolin plus metronidazole, or cefoxitin) are required for colorectal surgery.

Targeted preoperative MRSA screening and decolonization (nasal mupirocin 2% ointment twice daily for 5 days combined with daily 4% chlorhexidine body washes) prior to elective high-risk procedures (orthopedic arthroplasty and cardiac surgery) significantly reduces S. aureus surgical site infections; vancomycin is added to cefazolin only for confirmed MRSA carriers or high-risk institutional settings.

uncertainties: Universal versus targeted preoperative nasal mupirocin decolonization in community hospitals with low baseline MRSA prevalence.
Safety and allergy de-labeling protocols for utilizing cefazolin in patients with non-anaphylactic historical penicillin allergies.
mcq_angles: Timing window for standard antibiotic prophylaxis: complete infusion within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision; vancomycin requires 120 minutes due to Red Man syndrome.
Postoperative antibiotic duration rule: prophylactic antibiotics must be stopped within 24 hours post-op (or at wound closure); prolonged continuation is not guideline-adherent.
Cefazolin weight-based dosing: 2 g for patients <120 kg; increased to 3 g for patients weighing >=120 kg (or BMI >35).

A 70-year-old woman scheduled for elective coronary artery bypass grafting whose preoperative nasal swab is positive for Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

page.mentor_intro: Suspected melanoma needs urgent specialist assessment and complete excision biopsy. Dermoscopy improves accuracy, and Breslow thickness determines wide excision margins and sentinel node biopsy.

teaching_points.claim: Pigmented lesions with asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variegation, diameter of 6 mm or more or evolution (ABCDE), or an 'ugly duckling' lesion, warrant urgent suspected-cancer referral.
Diagnosis is by complete excision biopsy with a narrow (about 2 mm) margin; incisional or shave biopsy is avoided where possible because accurate Breslow thickness drives management.
Dermoscopy raises diagnostic accuracy; melanoma features include an atypical network, irregular globules, blue-white veil and regression structures.
Wide local excision margins depend on Breslow thickness: 1 cm for in situ to 1 mm tumours, and 1 to 2 cm for 1 to 2 mm, with 2 cm (2 to 3 cm in UK guidance) for tumours thicker than 2 mm.
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered for tumours of about 0.8 mm or thicker, or thinner with ulceration.

uncertainties: Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with suspected melanoma, non-melanoma skin cancer and urgent referral.

page.mentor_intro: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency requiring rapid, systematic diagnostic evaluation to confirm or exclude pulmonary vascular occlusion while avoiding unnecessary CT radiation and contrast-induced nephropathy. The YEARS algorithm streamlines diagnostic evaluation using three clinical criteria: clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), hemoptysis, and whether PE is the most likely diagnosis. Combined with clinical probability-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs, YEARS safely rules out PE without CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) in up to 50% of suspected presentations, and has been validated across special populations including pregnant patients.

teaching_points.claim: The YEARS algorithm consists of 3 clinical items: (1) clinical signs of DVT, (2) hemoptysis, and (3) PE most likely diagnosis; in patients with 0 YEARS criteria, a D-dimer threshold of <1000 ng/mL safely excludes PE without imaging.
In patients with >=1 YEARS criteria, the standard D-dimer threshold of <500 ng/mL (or age-adjusted cutoff: age x 10 in patients >50 years) is applied to rule out PE without CTPA.

The pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm safely excludes PE in pregnant women without CTPA using compression ultrasonography (CUS) and YEARS-adjusted D-dimer, avoiding fetal and maternal breast ionizing radiation.

When imaging is required, CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the definitive gold standard imaging modality, providing direct visualization of filling defects in pulmonary arterial branches down to subsegmental levels.

uncertainties: Clinical significance and necessity of therapeutic anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism (SSPE) without concurrent DVT in low-risk patients.
Diagnostic accuracy of ventilation-perfusion SPECT imaging versus low-dose CTPA in patients with severe renal impairment or severe contrast allergy.
mcq_angles: Application of the YEARS diagnostic thresholds: explaining why patients with zero criteria use a 1000 ng/mL cutoff whereas those with >=1 use 500 ng/mL.
Applying age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 ug/L for patients >50 years) in non-YEARS conventional algorithms to improve specificity in older adults.
Initial workup of suspected PE in pregnancy: bilateral lower extremity compression duplex ultrasound prior to thoracic radiation.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old woman taking oral contraceptives presents with mild pleuritic chest pain; she has no leg swelling, no hemoptysis, and muscular strain is deemed more likely (0 YEARS criteria); her D-dimer is 780 ng/mL.
A 26-week pregnant female presents with sudden dyspnoea and right leg calf swelling; the clinical team initiates the pregnancy-adapted YEARS diagnostic pathway.

page.mentor_intro: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery, caused by transient global cerebral hypoperfusion. Syncope is categorized etiologically into reflex (neurally mediated: vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus hypersensitivity), orthostatic hypotension (autonomic failure, volume depletion, drug-induced), and cardiac syncope (arrhythmic or structural). The initial clinical priority is identifying high-risk cardiac features—syncope during exertion, supine syncope, sudden palpitations preceding collapse, family history of premature sudden death, abnormal ECG, or known structural heart disease—which mandate urgent inpatient cardiac evaluation.

teaching_points.claim: Cardiac syncope (arrhythmic or structural heart disease) is the strongest independent predictor of sudden cardiac death and 1-year mortality, mandating immediate 12-lead ECG and urgent echocardiography whenever red flags are present.

A standard 12-lead ECG is mandatory in ALL patients presenting with syncope, screening for high-risk electrical abnormalities: prolonged or short QTc, Brugada pattern, pre-excitation (delta wave / WPW), bifascicular block, high-degree AV block, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (epsilon waves).

Vasovagal syncope (the most common cause in young, healthy individuals) is characterized by classic prodromal autonomic symptoms (lightheadedness, diaphoresis, pallor, nausea, warmth) triggered by prolonged standing, pain, emotional distress, or venepuncture.

Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed by a sustained drop in systolic BP >=20 mmHg and/or diastolic BP >=10 mmHg (or a fall in systolic to <90 mmHg) within 3 minutes of standing from a supine position, commonly exacerbated by polypharmacy (vasodilators, diuretics).

uncertainties: Diagnostic yield and cost-effectiveness of early insertable cardiac monitors (implantable loop recorders [ILRs]) compared to conventional Holter monitoring in unexplained recurrent syncope.
Efficacy of pacemaker implantation in older patients with recurrent refractory vasovagal syncope with documented cardioinhibitory asystole.
mcq_angles: Differentiating high-risk cardiac syncope (exertional, supine, sudden collapse without prodrome) from benign vasovagal syncope.
Recognizing high-risk ECG findings in unexplained syncope that warrant immediate admission and continuous telemetry monitoring.
Diagnostic criteria for orthostatic hypotension and identifying causative pharmacological agents.

page.mentor_intro: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) caused by global cerebral hypoperfusion, characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery. Differentiating benign orthostatic and reflex syncope from cardiac syncope requires systematic orthostatic vital sign measurement and risk stratification.

teaching_points.claim: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is defined as a sustained reduction in systolic blood pressure of >=20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of >=10 mmHg (or a fall in SBP to <90 mmHg) within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt to >=60 degrees.

Pathophysiological categories of orthostatic hypotension include: (1) Non-neurogenic (hypovolemia, dehydration, blood loss, vasodilating medications, diuretics, alcohol), and (2) Neurogenic (primary autonomic failure in Parkinson disease, Multiple System Atrophy, pure autonomic failure; or secondary autonomic neuropathy in diabetes, amyloidosis, autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy).

Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH) is characterized by an inadequate compensatory heart rate increase upon standing (typically <10–15 bpm rise despite severe hypotension) and postprandial/supine hypertension; diagnosis can be supported by measuring supine and standing plasma norepinephrine (failure of norepinephrine to double on standing confirms defective sympathetic efferent release).

Non-pharmacological interventions are foundational: review and deprescribe culprit antihypertensive medications, liberalize dietary fluid (2–2.5 L/day) and sodium intake (6–10 g/day), apply waist-high compression stockings and abdominal binders, elevate head of the bed 10–15 degrees at night, and teach physical counterpressure maneuvers (leg crossing, squatting).

Pharmacological therapy for refractory neurogenic orthostatic hypotension includes: Midodrine (selective peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic agonist), Droxidopa (norepinephrine prodrug), and Fludrocortisone (synthetic mineralocorticoid promoting renal sodium retention and plasma volume expansion; monitor for supine hypertension and hypokalemia).

uncertainties: Comparative long-term clinical efficacy and supine hypertension safety of droxidopa versus midodrine in multiple system atrophy.
Role of pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor augmenting autonomic ganglionic transmission) as monotherapy for orthostatic hypotension.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic criteria for orthostatic hypotension: sustained fall in SBP >=20 mmHg or DBP >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.
Distinguishing neurogenic from non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: neurogenic OH features blunted compensatory tachycardia (<10-15 bpm increase) due to baroreflex failure.
Fludrocortisone monitoring hazard: promotes volume expansion but exacerbates supine hypertension, predisposing to nocturnal stroke and congestive heart failure.

page.mentor_intro: Evaluation of syncope requires distinguishing benign reflex/orthostatic etiologies from life-threatening cardiogenic causes. Permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated for high-grade atrioventricular block, symptomatic sick sinus syndrome, and severe cardioinhibitory reflex syncope meeting strict diagnostic criteria.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnostic workup of syncope prioritizes distinguishing cardiac (arrhythmic or structural) causes from vasovagal and orthostatic syncope; persistent unexplained syncope in patients with underlying structural heart disease or abnormal baseline ECG carries high risk of sudden cardiac death.

Class I indications for permanent cardiac pacing in acquired atrioventricular (AV) block include complete third-degree AV block, advanced/high-grade second-degree AV block, and Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block, regardless of symptoms.

In sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction), pacing is indicated only when syncope or presyncope is directly documented to correlate with symptomatic sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, or sinoatrial exit block.

For recurrent cardioinhibitory reflex syncope in patients aged >=40 years, dual-chamber pacemaker implantation is indicated when documentation of asystolic pauses >=3 seconds (with syncope) or >=6 seconds (asymptomatic) is confirmed during tilt-table testing or implantable loop recorder (ILR) monitoring.

uncertainties: Efficacy of closed-loop stimulation (CLS) pacing versus conventional dual-chamber DDD pacing in suppressing vasovagal syncope recurrence.
Threshold for prophylactic pacemaker implantation in asymptomatic patients with alternating bundle branch block.

Pacing threshold in carotid sinus hypersensitivity: reproduction of syncope with asystole >3 seconds during carotid sinus massage confirms cardioinhibitory subtype.
Mobitz I vs Mobitz II pacing indications: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) usually does not require pacing unless symptomatic; Mobitz II always warrants permanent pacing.

page.mentor_intro: Synovial fluid arthrocentesis and analysis is the definitive diagnostic procedure for acute arthritis. Evaluating fluid appearance, leukocyte count, differential, polarized microscopy for crystals, and microbiological culture allows reliable differentiation of non-inflammatory, inflammatory, and septic joint pathology.

teaching_points.claim: Synovial fluid classification divides effusions into four major categories: (1) Normal (clear, viscous, WBC <200/uL), (2) Non-inflammatory (clear/yellow, viscous, WBC 200–2,000/uL with <25% PMNs; osteoarthritis, trauma), (3) Inflammatory (cloudy/translucent, low viscosity, WBC 2,000–50,000/uL with >50% PMNs; RA, gout, pseudogout, spondyloarthritis), and (4) Septic (opaque/purulent, low viscosity, WBC >50,000/uL with >75–90% PMNs).

Viscosity is high in normal and non-inflammatory fluid (forming a 3–5 cm string between fingers / 'string sign' due to intact high-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid), and is low/watery in inflammatory and septic states where bacterial and leukocyte hyaluronidases depolymerize hyaluronic acid.

Compensated polarized light microscopy differentiates crystal types: Monosodium Urate (MSU / gout) crystals are needle-shaped with strongly negative birefringence (appearing bright yellow when aligned parallel to the compensator axis and blue when perpendicular); Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate (CPPD / pseudogout) crystals are rhomboid/rod-shaped with weakly positive birefringence (appearing blue when aligned parallel and yellow when perpendicular).

Synovial fluid glucose is normally identical to serum glucose; in septic arthritis and severe rheumatoid arthritis, synovial glucose is markedly depressed (<50% of simultaneous blood glucose) due to leukocyte and bacterial consumption.

Microbiological culture: synovial fluid should be inoculated directly into blood culture bottles (aerobic and anaerobic) at the bedside, which significantly enhances bacterial recovery and yield compared to standard sterile specimen cups, particularly for fastidious organisms (Kingella kingae in children, Neisseria, and Streptococci).

uncertainties: Diagnostic utility of automated synovial fluid PCR syndromic panels in patients with suspected septic arthritis who received empiric antibiotics prior to arthrocentesis.
Significance of intracellular versus extracellular crystals in predicting true acute crystal-induced flare versus incidental background crystalluria.
mcq_angles: Compensated polarized light microscopy rules: Gout (MSU) = needle-shaped, strongly negative birefringence, yellow when parallel; Pseudogout (CPPD) = rhomboid, weakly positive birefringence, blue when parallel.
Synovial leukocyte cutoffs: Non-inflammatory = <2,000 WBC/uL; Inflammatory = 2,000–50,000 WBC/uL; Septic = >50,000 WBC/uL with >90% PMNs.
Blood culture bottle inoculation: direct bedside inoculation of synovial fluid into blood culture media dramatically increases culture sensitivity in septic arthritis.

page.mentor_intro: Syphilis is staged clinically, confirmed with treponemal and non-treponemal serology, and treated with benzathine penicillin G for early and late latent disease, and intravenous benzylpenicillin for neurosyphilis.

teaching_points.claim: Primary syphilis presents with a painless indurated chancre; secondary with a non-itchy rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata and lymphadenopathy.
Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent) is treated with a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM.
Late latent and tertiary syphilis (gummatous, cardiovascular) are treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks.

Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis are treated with IV benzylpenicillin 18 to 24 million units daily for 10 to 14 days; lumbar puncture is performed when neurological, ocular or otic features are present.
Diagnosis uses a treponemal test (EIA/TPPA) with a non-treponemal titre (RPR/VDRL); treatment response is a fourfold titre fall, and the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may follow the first dose.

page.mentor_intro: Syringomyelia is a neurological disorder characterized by the development of a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord parenchyma. Most commonly associated with Chiari I malformation, it presents with a classic dissociated sensory loss and requires neurosurgical restoration of normal cerebrospinal fluid dynamics.

teaching_points.claim: Syringomyelia most frequently results from obstruction to normal pulsatile cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow at the foramen magnum; Chiari I malformation (downward herniation of cerebellar tonsils >5 mm below the foramen magnum) accounts for >50–70% of non-traumatic syringomyelia cases.

Secondary non-Chiari etiologies include spinal cord trauma (post-traumatic syringomyelia developing months to years after injury), spinal arachnoiditis (infectious, post-surgical), spinal cord tumors (ependymoma, hemangioblastoma), and tethered cord syndrome.

The classic clinical presentation is a 'dissociated sensory loss' in a cape-like distribution across the shoulders, arms, and upper torso: loss of pain and temperature sensation with complete preservation of light touch, vibration, and proprioception, caused by the expanding syrinx disrupting crossing second-order spinothalamic neurons in the anterior white commissure.

Progression of the syrinx into anterior horn gray matter causes lower motor neuron weakness, muscle atrophy, and fasciculations in the hands and arms, while compression of lateral corticospinal tracts produces spastic paraparesis and hyperreflexia in the lower extremities; extension into the brainstem is termed syringobulbia (producing vocal cord paralysis, dysphagia, and tongue wasting).

Surgical management: Posterior Fossa Decompression (PFD—suboccipital craniectomy, C1 laminectomy, and duraplasty) is the primary definitive surgery for Chiari I-associated syringomyelia, restoring normal CSF dynamics at the craniovertebral junction and leading to syrinx collapse in >80% of cases; direct syrinx shunting (syringosubarachnoid or syringoperitoneal shunt) is reserved for non-communicating post-traumatic or post-inflammatory syringes refractory to decompression.

uncertainties: Management of asymptomatic, incidentally detected Chiari I malformations with small stable non-expansile syringes on cervical MRI.
Failure rates and optimal revision strategies for arachnoid scarring following previous posterior fossa duraplasty.
mcq_angles: Anatomical basis of dissociated sensory loss: selective destruction of decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, sparing dorsal columns (proprioception intact).
First-line surgical treatment for Chiari-associated syrinx: posterior fossa suboccipital craniectomy and duraplasty (restoring CSF flow); direct syrinx shunts are avoided as initial therapy.
Chiari I diagnostic MRI threshold: caudal herniation of one or both cerebellar tonsils >=5 mm below the level of the foramen magnum.

page.mentor_intro: Systemic analgesia forms the pharmacological backbone of acute and chronic pain management, integrating non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs), adjuvant agents (gabapentinoids, ketamine, alpha-2 agonists), and opioids. The World Health Organization (WHO) analgesic ladder and modern multimodal opioid-sparing protocols emphasize combining analgesics with distinct mechanisms of action to achieve synergistic pain relief while minimizing opioid-related adverse effects (hypoventilation, sedation, ileus, hyperalgesia, dependency). Safe administration requires tailoring drug selection and dosing to renal function, hepatic reserve, gastrointestinal bleeding risk, cardiovascular co-morbidities, and individual patient age.

teaching_points.claim: Multimodal systemic analgesia—combining paracetamol, NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors, and regional blocks—significantly reduces 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption and accelerates functional recovery compared to opioid monotherapy.

Intravenous non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., ketorolac) provide potent opioid-sparing analgesia, but are contraindicated in acute kidney injury, advanced CKD (eGFR <30), active gastrointestinal ulceration, active bleeding, and immediately prior to high-risk vascular or spinal surgeries.

Low-dose sub-dissociative ketamine infusions (0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg/h) provide potent NMDA receptor antagonism, reducing severe postoperative opioid tolerance, hyperalgesia, and chronic postsurgical pain syndromes without inducing psychomimetic side effects.

Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) with IV morphine, hydromorphone, or fentanyl provides superior patient satisfaction and analgesia over intermittent nurse-administered boluses; routine continuous basal infusions should be avoided in opioid-naive patients to prevent fatal nocturnal respiratory depression.

uncertainties: Role and optimal duration of perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusions in non-abdominal surgical cohorts.
Comparative long-term safety and persistent post-surgical pain prevention with perioperative gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) given recent concerns over respiratory depression.
mcq_angles: Risks of routine basal rate infusions in intravenous opioid patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) in opioid-naive adults (increased risk of life-threatening respiratory depression).
Mechanisms and indications of sub-dissociative ketamine infusions in managing acute severe pain and opioid-tolerant patients.
Absolute contraindications to systemic NSAIDs in acute perioperative and critically ill clinical settings.

page.mentor_intro: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a prototypical systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by loss of self-tolerance, immune complex deposition, and multiorgan inflammation predominantly affecting women of childbearing age (9:1 female-to-male ratio). Clinical manifestations range from cutaneous lesions (malar rash, discoid lupus), non-erosive polyarthritis, and serositis, to life-threatening lupus nephritis, neuropsychiatric lupus, and severe haematologic cytopenias. Treatment paradigms emphasize early hydroxychloroquine for all patients (improving survival and preventing flares), strict glucocorticoid tapering, and early integration of immunosuppressives and targeted biologics (belimumab, anifrolumab).

teaching_points.claim: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is recommended for ALL patients with systemic lupus erythematosus unless contraindicated, dosed at <=5 mg/kg actual body weight daily to reduce mortality, prevent organ flares, and minimize retinal toxicity risks.

Antinuclear antibody (ANA) tested by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells possesses >98% sensitivity, serving as the essential entry criterion in the 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria; a negative ANA strongly argues against idiopathic SLE.

Lupus nephritis (occurring in up to 50% of patients) requires prompt diagnostic renal biopsy for ISN/RPS histologic classification (Class I through VI); Class III (focal) and Class IV (diffuse proliferative) nephritis carry highest risk of end-stage renal disease and mandate intensive induction with mycophenolate mofetil or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids.

Targeted biologic therapies—belimumab (anti-BAFF/BLyS) and anifrolumab (anti-type I interferon receptor monoclonal antibody)—significantly reduce disease activity, enable corticosteroid tapering, and prevent systemic disease flares in active SLE.

uncertainties: Efficacy of upfront triple therapy (mycophenolate mofetil, calcineurin inhibitors [voclosporin], and belimumab) in severe proliferative lupus nephritis.
Safety and feasibility of complete withdrawal of maintenance glucocorticoid therapy in patients achieving long-term serological and clinical remission.
mcq_angles: Universal indication and safe weight-based dosing threshold for hydroxychloroquine (<=5 mg/kg actual body weight) and retinal screening protocols.
Identifying high-risk lupus nephritis (Class III/IV) requiring aggressive immunosuppressive induction with mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide.
Interpretation of ANA, anti-dsDNA, and anti-Smith autoantibodies (anti-dsDNA correlates with nephritis activity and complement consumption; anti-Sm is highly specific).

page.mentor_intro: Biologic therapies in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) provide targeted immunosuppression directed at pathogenic B-cell survival factors and type I interferon signaling pathways. Integrating approved biologics alongside conventional synthetic therapy enables corticosteroid minimization and durable clinical remission.

teaching_points.claim: Belimumab—a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds and neutralizes soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS / BAFF)—was the first targeted biologic approved for active autoantibody-positive SLE; it inhibits B-cell survival and differentiation, significantly reducing SLE disease flares and corticosteroid requirements (BLISS trials).

In active lupus nephritis (LN), the landmark BLISS-LN trial demonstrated that adding belimumab to standard induction therapy (mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide) significantly improved primary efficacy renal response and reduced the risk of renal-related events or death.

Anifrolumab—a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting the type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1)—blocks the downstream biological activity of all type I interferons (IFN-alpha, IFN-beta); the TULIP trials established that anifrolumab significantly improves composite skin and musculoskeletal disease activity in active moderate-to-severe SLE.

Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) is utilized off-label as evidence-based therapy for severe, refractory lupus manifestations: refractory Class III/IV lupus nephritis, severe immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), and central nervous system neuropsychiatric lupus.

Targeted biologic therapy allows substantial glucocorticoid minimization: international EULAR guidelines establish a clinical target of tapering maintenance prednisone to <=5 mg/day (or complete withdrawal) to prevent irreversible cumulative organ damage.

uncertainties: Efficacy of dual B-cell targeted therapy (sequential rituximab followed by belimumab) in preventing compensatory BLyS surges and sustaining remission in severe lupus nephritis.
Risk of herpes zoster reactivation during anifrolumab therapy and optimal timing for recombinant zoster vaccination (Shingrix).
mcq_angles: Belimumab molecular target: binds soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS/BAFF) to inhibit autoreactive B-cell survival and autoantibody production.
Anifrolumab mechanism of action: blocks type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1), dampening the pathogenic interferon gene signature in SLE.
BLISS-LN trial clinical impact: adding belimumab to standard induction therapy improves complete renal response and slows renal function decline in lupus nephritis.
case_hooks: A 32-year-old woman with active SLE experiencing persistent polyarthritis, malar rash, and positive anti-dsDNA despite hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate, started on IV belimumab.
A 28-year-old woman with refractory biopsy-proven Class IV lupus nephritis on mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone who receives add-on B-cell depletion with rituximab.

page.mentor_intro: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is a multisystem autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by a triad of microvascular obliterative vasculopathy, systemic immune activation with autoantibody production, and widespread progressive tissue fibrosis of skin and internal organs.

teaching_points.claim: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is broadly classified into two major cutaneous subsets: Limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc, formerly CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia; skin thickening restricted to hands, face, and distal elbows/knees) and Diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc: rapid skin thickening extending proximally to trunk and thighs, carrying high early visceral organ failure risk).

Autoantibody profiles strongly correlate with clinical phenotypes: Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are classic for lcSSc (associated with severe Raynaud's, digital ulcers, and late development of isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension [PAH]); Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) is characteristic of dcSSc (strongly associated with progressive pulmonary fibrosis / SSc-ILD); Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are linked to rapidly progressive diffuse skin disease and a high risk of scleroderma renal crisis.

Raynaud phenomenon is the universal early presenting sign (>95% of patients); nailfold capillaroscopy is an essential diagnostic tool revealing early microvascular architectural changes: dilated giant capillary loops, microhemorrhages, and progressive capillary loss/avascular areas.

Leading causes of mortality in modern systemic sclerosis are pulmonary complications: Interstitial Lung Disease (SSc-ILD, developing in up to 80% of dcSSc) and Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH, developing in 10–15% of lcSSc); baseline high-resolution CT of the chest, pulmonary function tests with DLCO, and annual screening echocardiography are mandatory.

Targeted organ-specific pharmacotherapy: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) and PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) for Raynaud's and digital ulcers; mycophenolate mofetil or nintedanib for active SSc-ILD; oral captopril for scleroderma renal crisis; and ERA/PDE-5i combinations for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

uncertainties: Therapeutic role and patient selection criteria for autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in severe, rapidly progressive diffuse systemic sclerosis.
Clinical utility of novel antifibrotic and anti-IL-6 combinations in slowing multi-organ dermal and pulmonary fibrosis.
mcq_angles: Antibody-phenotype correlations: Anti-Scl-70 predicts interstitial lung disease; anti-centromere predicts late pulmonary arterial hypertension; anti-RNA polymerase III predicts scleroderma renal crisis.
Leading causes of death: pulmonary involvement (SSc-ILD and PAH) has surpassed renal crisis as the primary cause of scleroderma mortality.
Diagnostic utility of nailfold capillaroscopy: detects giant enlarged capillary loops and avascular drop-out areas, distinguishing primary Raynaud from secondary autoimmune systemic sclerosis.
case_hooks: A 42-year-old woman presenting with severe cold-induced digital triphasic color changes, sclerodactyly of both hands, facial telangiectasias, and positive anti-centromere antibodies.

A 38-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma and anti-Scl-70 antibodies presenting with progressive exertional dyspnea and bibasilar crackles, whose HRCT shows non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP).

page.mentor_intro: Systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD) is the leading cause of mortality in systemic sclerosis, affecting up to 80% of patients on imaging. Early screening with high-resolution chest CT and pulmonary function tests guides timely combination immunosuppression and antifibrotic therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) occurs in both diffuse and limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, with the highest prevalence and most rapid progression occurring in patients with dcSSc, male sex, older age, and anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) autoantibodies.

High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest is mandatory at baseline for all patients with systemic sclerosis; the predominant radiological and histological pattern in SSc-ILD is Non-Specific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP, present in 70–80%), characterized by bilateral, symmetric, basilar ground-glass opacities with traction bronchiectasis and relative subpleural sparing; UIP pattern occurs in 15–20%.

The Scleroderma Lung Study I and II (SLS I and II) established Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF, target 2 to 3 g daily) as the preferred first-line immunosuppressive agent for active SSc-ILD, demonstrating equivalent stabilization of forced vital capacity (FVC) with vastly superior safety and tolerability compared to oral cyclophosphamide.

In patients with progressive fibrosing SSc-ILD, the landmark SENSCIS trial demonstrated that adding the antifibrotic tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib (150 mg twice daily) to baseline therapy significantly reduced the annual rate of decline in FVC by 44% (annual decline of -52.4 mL/year with nintedanib vs -93.3 mL/year with placebo, P=0.04).

The anti-IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab (focuSSced trial) demonstrated preservation of lung function in patients with early diffuse cutaneous SSc with elevated inflammatory markers, earning regulatory approval for slowing FVC decline in SSc-ILD.

uncertainties: Optimal threshold for combining upfront immunosuppression (MMF) with antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) versus sequential add-on upon documented FVC progression.
Role of cyclophosphamide rescue followed by autologous stem cell transplantation in rapidly progressive SSc-ILD refractory to MMF.
mcq_angles: Predominant HRCT pattern in SSc-ILD: Non-Specific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP) with bilateral basal ground-glass opacities and subpleural sparing, contrasting with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (UIP).
First-line immunosuppressive of choice: mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is the preferred standard first-line agent based on the Scleroderma Lung Study II.
SENSCIS trial landmark outcome: nintedanib (antifibrotic TKI) significantly reduces the annual rate of FVC decline in systemic sclerosis-associated ILD.
case_hooks: A 46-year-old woman with newly diagnosed diffuse systemic sclerosis and anti-Scl-70 antibodies whose baseline HRCT demonstrates bibasilar ground-glass opacities with an FVC of 72% predicted.
A 52-year-old woman with SSc-ILD on maintenance mycophenolate mofetil who exhibits a 6% decline in FVC over 12 months, evaluated for combination therapy with nintedanib.
