page.mentor_intro: Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is a rare, chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting the aorta, its primary branches, and the pulmonary arteries, most commonly presenting in young females under 40 years of age. Inflammatory panarteritis leads to wall thickening, luminal stenosis, occlusion, and aneurysm formation, manifesting clinically as absent peripheral pulses, vascular bruits, limb claudication, and severe renovascular hypertension. While high-dose corticosteroids achieve initial remission, over 50% of patients relapse upon steroid tapering; biologic therapies—particularly TNF inhibitors and IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab)—serve as essential steroid-sparing agents for refractory or relapsing disease.

teaching_points.claim: First-line induction therapy for active Takayasu arteritis utilizes high-dose systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day); however, early addition of a steroid-sparing disease-modifying agent is mandatory due to high relapse rates during steroid taper.

Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) and the anti-IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab demonstrate substantial efficacy in inducing clinical remission, halting angiographic disease progression, and permitting major corticosteroid dose reduction in refractory Takayasu arteritis.

Assessment of vascular disease activity requires specialized non-invasive vascular imaging (contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiography [MRA], CT angiography, or 18F-FDG PET/CT), as acute phase reactants (ESR, CRP) can be completely normal in up to 30-40% of patients with histologically active vascular inflammation.

Revascularization procedures (percutaneous angioplasty, stenting, or bypass surgery) must strictly be avoided during active vessel inflammation, as operating on inflamed vessels carries catastrophic risks of thrombosis, anastomotic disruption, and restenosis; procedures must be delayed until medical remission is achieved.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term efficacy and vascular wall remodeling between anti-TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab in paediatric-onset Takayasu arteritis.
Role of Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (e.g., tofacitinib) in patients failing both TNF and IL-6 targeted biologic agents.
mcq_angles: Selection of biologic therapies (anti-TNF agents vs tocilizumab) in steroid-refractory Takayasu arteritis.
Timing of surgical or catheter-based vascular interventions: absolute requirement to induce stable immunosuppressive remission prior to elective revascularization.
Limitations of acute phase reactants (ESR/CRP) in monitoring disease activity, highlighting the necessity of serial MRA or FDG-PET imaging.

A 28-year-old woman with active Takayasu arteritis relapses with progressive subclavian artery stenosis every time prednisone is tapered below 20 mg daily; the rheumatologist initiates biologic therapy with tocilizumab.

page.mentor_intro: Takayasu's arteritis ('pulseless disease') is a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis primarily affecting the aorta, its primary branches, and the pulmonary arteries in young females. Transmural inflammation leads to arterial stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm formation, and limb claudication, requiring early immunosuppression.

teaching_points.claim: Takayasu's arteritis predominantly affects young women (female-to-male ratio 8:1 to 9:1, typically presenting before age 40); transmural granulomatous inflammation of the aorta and major branch vessels leads to marked arterial wall thickening, luminal stenosis, thrombosis, and post-stenotic aneurysm formation.

Clinical presentation classically follows a biphasic course: an initial 'pre-pulseless' systemic inflammatory phase (fever, night sweats, fatigue, arthralgias, weight loss) followed by a late 'pulseless' occlusive vascular phase (upper limb claudication, asymmetric blood pressures [>10 mmHg difference between arms], absent peripheral pulses, carotidynia, vascular bruits, and lightheadedness).

Diagnostic vascular imaging of choice is contrast-enhanced Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) or CT Angiography (CTA) of the entire aorta and its branches, or 18F-FDG PET-CT; imaging demonstrates concentric, circumferential arterial wall thickening, wall edema, delayed contrast enhancement, and luminal stenosis/occlusion.

First-line medical induction therapy is high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, typically 40–60 mg daily); however, relapses occur in >50% of patients during steroid tapering, mandating early co-administration of steroid-sparing conventional synthetic immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, or leflunomide).

In patients with refractory or relapsing large-vessel vasculitis, biologic therapy with TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) or the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab demonstrates proven efficacy in achieving sustained clinical remission and arresting arterial structural progression.

Surgical or endovascular revascularization (bypass grafting, percutaneous transluminal angioplasty) must be strictly avoided during active acute vascular inflammation due to catastrophic risks of graft thrombosis, anastomotic disruption, and pseudoaneurysm formation; revascularization should be performed electively only after stable immunosuppressive-induced disease remission is achieved.

uncertainties: Diagnostic accuracy of serum biomarkers (e.g., pentraxin-3, matrix metalloproteinases) versus 18F-FDG PET-CT in monitoring subclinical intramural vascular inflammation.
Optimal long-term antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet vs anticoagulation) in patients with extensive large-vessel stenoses and aneurysms.
mcq_angles: Surgical timing rule in Takayasu arteritis: vascular revascularization must NEVER be performed during active vascular inflammation; postpone until complete clinical and biochemical remission is achieved.
Physical examination hallmarks: asymmetric blood pressure (>10 mmHg discrepancy between arms), diminished or absent radial pulses, and arterial bruits over carotids, subclavians, or abdominal aorta.
Biologic therapy of choice for refractory disease: TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab) or IL-6 receptor blockade (tocilizumab) significantly reduce steroid requirements and vascular progression.

page.mentor_intro: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced cardiomyopathy / 'broken heart syndrome') is a transient acute myocardial syndrome mimicking acute coronary syndrome. Characteristically triggered by severe physical or emotional stressors in postmenopausal women, management focuses on supportive hemodynamics and managing complications.

teaching_points.claim: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is characterized by acute, transient left ventricular systolic dysfunction with regional wall motion abnormalities that typically extend beyond the distribution of a single epicardial coronary artery, accompanied by electrocardiographic changes and mild cardiac biomarker elevation mimicking STEMI.

Pathophysiology is mediated by massive sympathetic nervous system activation and a surge in circulating catecholamines, which triggers microvascular coronary spasm, direct myocyte catecholamine toxicity, and functional myocardial stunning via high-affinity beta-2 adrenergic receptor Gs-to-Gi pathway switching.

Diagnostic criteria (InterTAK Diagnostic Criteria / Mayo Clinic criteria) require: (1) Transient LV regional wall motion abnormalities (apical ballooning [classic in 80%], midventricular, basal, or focal variants), (2) Absence of culprit obstructive coronary atherothrombosis or acute plaque rupture on emergency coronary angiography, (3) New ECG abnormalities (ST-segment elevation, T-wave inversion, prolonged QTc), and (4) Modest troponin elevation disproportionately low relative to the extensive extent of LV wall motion dysfunction.

Complications develop in up to 20% of patients and include: left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction with dynamic systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve, acute cardiogenic shock, apical mural thrombus formation, lethal ventricular arrhythmias (associated with severe QTc prolongation >500 ms), and heart failure.

In patients who develop cardiogenic shock with dynamic LVOT obstruction, inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone, adrenaline) are strictly CONTRAINDICATED as they worsen the intraventricular pressure gradient; management requires IV fluid hydration, beta-blocker titration, and pure alpha-1 vasoconstrictors (phenylephrine or noradrenaline); in refractory shock without LVOT obstruction, mechanical circulatory support (Impella or VA-ECMO) provides hemodynamic rescue.

uncertainties: Efficacy of chronic long-term beta-blocker or ACE inhibitor therapy in preventing late recurrences (recurrence rate approx. 1-2% per year).
Optimal duration of prophylactic therapeutic anticoagulation in patients with severe apical ballooning and akinesia to prevent apical thrombus formation.
mcq_angles: Inotrope contraindication in Takotsubo LVOT obstruction: inotropes (dobutamine) worsen systolic anterior motion (SAM) and intraventricular pressure gradients; beta-blockers and gentle fluids are indicated.

page.mentor_intro: Targeted temperature management (TTM) is a core neuroprotective strategy for comatose survivors of cardiac arrest. landmark trials have established that preventing fever and maintaining strict normothermia (36.0 to 37.5 C) provides neurological outcomes and survival equivalent to hypothermia (33 C).

teaching_points.claim: Targeted temperature management (TTM) is indicated for adult patients who remain comatose (unresponsive or not following commands) after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) following out-of-hospital or in-hospital cardiac arrest, regardless of initial cardiac rhythm.

The landmark TTM2 randomized controlled trial (1,900 patients) demonstrated that targeted hypothermia at 33 C did NOT reduce all-cause mortality or improve functional neurological outcomes at 6 months compared with targeted normothermia (maintaining core temperature <=37.5 C with active device warming/cooling), while hypothermia caused significantly higher rates of cardiac arrhythmias requiring intervention.

Current international guidelines (ILCOR, AHA, ERC) recommend maintaining a constant target temperature between 32.0 C and 37.5 C for at least 24 hours post-ROSC; active prevention and treatment of fever (temperature >=37.8 C) is mandatory for at least 72 hours post-cardiac arrest.

Temperature control must be achieved using dedicated closed-loop feedback systems (intravascular cooling catheters or surface cooling pads with automated water circulation) coupled to continuous core temperature monitoring (esophageal, bladder, or intravascular probe).

Multimodal neuroprognostication must be delayed until at least 72 hours post-arrest (or 72 hours after rewarming/normothermia) to avoid confounding by sedatives and hypothermia: evaluating bilateral absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20 somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP) waves, high serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE >60 ug/L at 48-72h), and status myoclonus.

uncertainties: Subgroup benefits of deeper hypothermia (33 C) in specific high-severity arrest phenotypes (e.g., prolonged downtime or severe post-ischemic brain swelling).
Optimal rewarming speed and shivering control protocols during automated temperature feedback management.
mcq_angles: TTM2 trial landmark outcome: hypothermia at 33 C does NOT improve survival or neurological recovery compared to targeted normothermia (<=37.5 C) in post-cardiac arrest coma.
Fever prevention duration: actively prevent fever (temperature >=37.8 C) for at least 72 hours post-ROSC in comatose cardiac arrest patients.
Neuroprognostication timing standard: multimodal neurological prognostication must be deferred until at least 72 hours after cardiac arrest to prevent premature withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy.
case_hooks: A 56-year-old man resuscitated from out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest who remains intubated and comatose (GCS 3T) in the ICU, placed on an automated surface cooling feedback protocol set to 36.5 C.
A 62-year-old comatose cardiac arrest patient at 72 hours post-ROSC evaluated with SSEP, EEG, and serum neuron-specific enolase.

page.mentor_intro: Targeted cancer therapy utilizes drugs designed to interfere with specific molecular pathways, mutated oncoproteins, or cell-surface receptors driving tumor growth and survival. Understanding predictive biomarkers, mechanism of action, and secondary resistance mechanisms forms the core of modern precision oncology.

teaching_points.claim: Targeted therapies are broadly categorized into two major pharmacological classes: (1) Small-molecule inhibitors (suffix '-nib': e.g., osimertinib, imatinib), which are orally bioavailable and penetrate the cell membrane to inhibit intracellular kinase catalytic domains, and (2) Monoclonal antibodies (suffix '-mab': e.g., trastuzumab, rituximab, cetuximab), which are large macromolecules administered intravenously that bind extracellular cell-surface receptors or circulating ligands.

Therapy must be guided by validated predictive biomarkers: testing must confirm the presence of the specific molecular target before drug administration (e.g., EGFR exon 19 deletions / L858R for osimertinib; BRAF V600E mutations for dabrafenib; HER2 overexpression/amplification for trastuzumab; BCR-ABL1 fusion for imatinib).

Targeted therapies exhibit a fundamentally different toxicity profile compared with cytotoxic chemotherapy: instead of alopecia and myelosuppression, adverse effects are mechanism-specific (e.g., acneiform papulopustular skin rash and diarrhea with EGFR inhibitors; hypertension, proteinuria, and impaired wound healing with VEGF inhibitors; hepatotoxicity with multi-kinase TKIs).

Secondary acquired resistance inevitably develops through Darwinian clonal selection: mechanisms include on-target secondary gatekeeper mutations in the kinase domain (e.g., EGFR T790M or C797S mutations, BCR-ABL T315I mutation), bypass signaling pathway activation (MET amplification in EGFR-mutant lung cancer), phenotypic histological transformation (adenocarcinoma to small-cell lung cancer), or loss of target expression.

Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs—e.g., trastuzumab deruxtecan [T-DXd], sacituzumab govitecan) combine the antigen-specificity of a monoclonal antibody with the cytotoxic potency of a membrane-permeable payload (topoisomerase I inhibitor or microtubule disruptor) via a cleavable linker, exerting potent 'bystander killing' on neighboring antigen-negative tumor cells.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing of next-generation covalent allosteric inhibitors versus antibody-drug conjugates following progression on frontline targeted therapies.
Role of serial circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) liquid biopsies in preemptively detecting emergent resistance mutations prior to radiographic progression.
mcq_angles: Small molecule versus monoclonal antibody distinction: small molecules ('-nib') inhibit intracellular catalytic domains; monoclonal antibodies ('-mab') bind extracellular surface receptors or circulating ligands.
EGFR inhibitor class toxicity: papulopustular acneiform rash, paronychia, and diarrhea; rash severity positively correlates with therapeutic tumor response.
Antibody-Drug Conjugate (ADC) bystander effect: membrane-permeable cytotoxic payloads diffuse out of the targeted cell to destroy adjacent heterogeneous tumor cells lacking target expression.
case_hooks: A 54-year-old non-smoking woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma whose tumor next-generation sequencing reveals an EGFR exon 19 deletion, initiated on first-line osimertinib.
A 60-year-old woman with metastatic HER2-low breast cancer receiving trastuzumab deruxtecan who achieves a partial tumor response.

page.mentor_intro: Tuberculosis (TB) screening aims to identify active tuberculosis disease and detect latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) in individuals at high risk of disease reactivation. Targeted screening of immunocompromised hosts, healthcare workers, contacts, and immigrants prevents transmission and clinical disease.

teaching_points.claim: Screening for Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) is indicated prior to initiating biologic therapies (especially TNF-alpha inhibitors), before solid organ or stem cell transplantation, in HIV infection, in close contacts of active pulmonary TB cases, and in recent immigrants from high-incidence countries.

Diagnostic tests for LTBI include Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRAs: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, T-SPOT.TB) and the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST / Mantoux test); IGRAs measure in vitro interferon-gamma release by T cells stimulated with specific M. tuberculosis antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP-10).

IGRAs possess significantly superior diagnostic specificity (>95%) compared to TST in individuals who have received the Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine, as ESAT-6 and CFP-10 antigens are absent from the BCG vaccine strain and most non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), eliminating false-positive BCG cross-reactions.

Tuberculin skin test (TST) interpretation criteria for induration at 48 to 72 hours: >=5 mm is positive in high-risk individuals (HIV-positive, recent TB contacts, organ transplant, immunosuppressed on prednisone >=15 mg/day); >=10 mm is positive in moderate-risk individuals (recent immigrants <5 years, IV drug users, healthcare workers, diabetic/ESRD); >=15 mm is positive in low-risk individuals with no known risk factors.

Any positive IGRA or TST mandates a chest radiograph and systematic symptom evaluation to strictly exclude active pulmonary tuberculosis before initiating LTBI treatment; modern preferred LTBI regimens include short-course rifamycin-based therapies: 3 months of once-weekly oral rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP), 4 months of daily rifampin (4R), or 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin (3HR).

uncertainties: Diagnostic reliability and indeterminate rate of IGRAs in patients with severe peripheral lymphopenia (CD4 count <100/uL).
Optimal screening frequency and cost-effectiveness of annual serial IGRA testing in healthcare workers in low-incidence settings.
mcq_angles: IGRA advantage over TST: IGRAs do not cross-react with BCG vaccination, providing high specificity in BCG-vaccinated populations.
Mandatory step following positive LTBI screening: perform chest radiography to rule out active pulmonary tuberculosis before commencing preventive therapy.
Preferred short-course LTBI treatment regimen: 3 months of once-weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP) or 4 months of daily rifampin (4R), replacing legacy 9-month isoniazid monotherapy.

page.mentor_intro: TB treatment: RIPE regimen, hepatotoxicity monitoring, directly observed therapy, drug-resistant TB is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Advances in tuberculosis treatment: novel regimens, new drug pipelines, host-directed therapies, and updated management guidelines.

Standard first-line therapy for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis comprises a 2-month intensive phase with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE), followed by a 4-month continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid (RI).

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) requires withholding hepatotoxic drugs (pyrazinamide > isoniazid > rifampicin) if serum transaminases exceed 5 times the upper limit of normal (or 3 times ULN with symptoms of jaundice, nausea, or abdominal pain).

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 25-50 mg daily) is routinely co-administered with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in patients with diabetes, alcohol dependence, renal failure, malnutrition, or pregnancy.

uncertainties: Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with tb treatment: ripe regimen, hepatotoxicity monitoring, directly observed therapy, drug-resistant tb.
Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

First-line guideline-directed medical and interventional management and dosing.

page.mentor_intro: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) and Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCL) are rare, heterogeneous non-Hodgkin lymphomas arising from mature post-thymic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells. Characterized by aggressive clinical behavior and poorer outcomes than B-cell lymphomas, personalized immunophenotypic and molecular classification dictates therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) represent approximately 10–15% of all non-Hodgkin lymphomas, comprising major clinical subtypes: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS), Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL), and Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL, ALK-positive vs ALK-negative).

ALK status in systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is the single most important prognostic factor: ALK-positive ALCL (driven by the t(2;5) translocation fusing NPM1 and ALK genes) occurs in younger patients and carries a favorable 5-year overall survival (>70–80%), whereas ALK-negative ALCL carries a significantly poorer prognosis.

The landmark ECHELON-2 randomized trial established frontline therapy for CD30-expressing peripheral T-cell lymphomas: brentuximab vedotin (an antibody-drug conjugate targeting CD30 linked to monomethyl auristatin E) combined with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisone (A+CHP) significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival compared with standard CHOP chemotherapy.

For fit patients with nodal PTCL (excluding ALK-positive ALCL) achieving a complete first remission, consolidation with high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) is guideline-recommended to prevent early relapse.

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL—predominantly Mycosis Fungoides and Sezary Syndrome) presents with cutaneous patches, plaques, and tumors; Sezary syndrome is the leukemic variant characterized by the triad of erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating clonally identical neoplastic T cells with cerebriform nuclei ('Sezary cells') in peripheral blood, treated with targeted agents like mogamulizumab (anti-CCR4).

uncertainties: Efficacy of targeted epigenetic therapies (histone deacetylase inhibitors romidepsin, belinostat; and DNA methyltransferase inhibitors) in angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma.
Role of allogeneic stem cell transplantation versus novel targeted CAR-T cellular therapies in relapsed/refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma.
mcq_angles: ECHELON-2 trial landmark finding: brentuximab vedotin plus CHP (A+CHP) is superior to CHOP for CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphomas (including ALCL).
Prognostic impact of ALK translocation in ALCL: ALK-positive ALCL carries an excellent prognosis with high cure rates compared to ALK-negative disease.
Sezary syndrome clinical triad: pruritic erythroderma covering >80% BSA, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T-cells with cerebriform nuclei.

page.mentor_intro: Temporal arteritis—also known as giant cell arteritis (GCA)—is the most prevalent systemic vasculitis in adults aged >50 years, characterized by granulomatous inflammation targeting large and medium-sized arteries, particularly the ophthalmic, temporal, and cranial branches of the external carotid artery, as well as the aorta. The paramount clinical concern is irreversible visual loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION), occurring in up to 15-20% of untreated patients. High-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy must be instituted immediately upon clinical suspicion, without waiting for temporal artery biopsy or vascular ultrasonography.

teaching_points.claim: High-dose systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone 40-60 mg daily, or IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for 3 days if visual symptoms or amaurosis fugax are present) must be initiated IMMEDIATELY upon suspicion of GCA to prevent irreversible blindness.

Temporal artery biopsy (TAB, with a minimum specimen length of >=1-2 cm due to 'skip lesions') remains the histological gold standard, but high-resolution temporal artery color Doppler ultrasound showing the non-compressible hypoechoic 'halo sign' (vessel wall oedema) has high sensitivity and specificity in experienced centers.

Classic clinical hallmarks include new-onset localized headache, scalp tenderness (pain when combing hair), jaw claudication (high specificity for vascular ischemia of the masseter muscles), polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) symptoms, and markedly elevated ESR (often >50-100 mm/h) and CRP.

Tocilizumab (monoclonal antibody targeting the IL-6 receptor) administered subcutaneously weekly or biweekly significantly increases sustained glucocorticoid-free remission and reduces cumulative steroid exposure and toxicity (GiACTA trial).

uncertainties: Duration of maintenance tocilizumab therapy (1 year versus extended multi-year therapy) to prevent relapse upon discontinuation.
Diagnostic utility of 18F-FDG PET/CT in detecting isolated large-vessel extracranial GCA (aortitis, subclavian arteritis) in patients with normal temporal artery imaging.
mcq_angles: Immediate management of suspected GCA with transient visual loss (emergency IV pulse methylprednisolone before obtaining biopsy).
Pathognomonic vascular ultrasound feature: identifying the hypoechoic 'halo sign' representing arterial wall inflammation and oedema.
Evidence for tocilizumab as an FDA/EMA-approved steroid-sparing agent in GCA from the GiACTA trial.

page.mentor_intro: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most common form of drug-resistant focal epilepsy in adults, frequently caused by mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS). In patients with medically refractory TLE, early surgical intervention with anterior temporal lobectomy achieves long-term seizure freedom and stops cognitive decline.

teaching_points.claim: Mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS / hippocampal sclerosis) is the most frequent underlying structural pathology in temporal lobe epilepsy, pathologically characterized by selective neuronal loss and severe astrogliosis in the CA1 and CA4 subfields and dentate gyrus of the hippocampus with relative preservation of CA2.

High-resolution epilepsy-protocol MRI is the definitive imaging modality, characteristically demonstrating hippocampal volume loss (atrophy) on T1-weighted sequences and hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences.

Classic clinical semiology features an epigastric rising aura ('butterflies in stomach'), psychic auras (deja vu, jamais vu, intense fear), olfactory/gustatory hallucinations, followed by behavioral arrest, staring, prominent oroalimentary automatisms (lip smacking, chewing, swallowing), manual automatisms (fumbling, picking), and contralateral dystonic limb posturing.

Drug-resistant epilepsy is defined as failure of adequate trials of two tolerated and appropriately chosen antiseizure medications (as monotherapy or in combination) to achieve sustained seizure freedom; in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, early surgical referral should not be delayed.

In the landmark randomized controlled trial by Wiebe et al. (NEJM), anterior temporal lobectomy (ATL) combined with medical therapy was vastly superior to continued medical therapy alone, achieving complete seizure freedom in 58% of surgically treated patients compared with only 8% in the medical group (P<0.001); superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky' visual field defect) is an expected postoperative anatomical risk due to disruption of Meyer's loop.

uncertainties: Comparative cognitive and verbal memory outcomes of selective amygdalohippocampectomy or MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) versus open anterior temporal lobectomy.
Long-term psychiatric outcomes (depression, anxiety, psychosis) following successful temporal lobe resection.
mcq_angles: Wiebe et al. trial landmark finding: anterior temporal lobectomy achieves significantly superior seizure freedom (~58% vs 8%) over continued medical therapy in drug-resistant TLE.
Postoperative visual field complication of anterior temporal lobectomy: contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky' defect) caused by disruption of Meyer's loop in temporal white matter.
MRI hallmark of mesial temporal sclerosis: unilateral hippocampal atrophy on T1 and increased signal hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR images.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old woman with a childhood history of prolonged febrile seizures presenting with rising epigastric auras, lip-smacking automatisms, and refractory seizures despite levetiracetam and lamotrigine.
A 34-year-old man who achieves complete seizure freedom following left anterior temporal lobectomy, undergoing routine post-surgical visual field perimetry.

page.mentor_intro: Tendinopathy describes a clinical syndrome of pain, localized swelling, and impaired performance in and around a tendon, characterized histopathologically by non-inflammatory tendon dysrepair, collagen fiber disorganization, mucoid ground substance increase, and neurovascular ingrowth (failed healing response). Common anatomical sites include the Achilles, patellar, rotator cuff, and common extensor tendons of the elbow (lateral epicondylalgia). The foundation of evidence-based conservative management is progressive mechanical tendon loading exercise (heavy slow resistance and eccentric training), with structured load management prioritizing long-term remodeling over passive interventions.

teaching_points.claim: Histopathology of chronic tendinopathy demonstrates tendon dysrepair, hypercellularity, neurovascular ingrowth, and collagen disorganization without acute inflammatory cells; the historic term 'tendinitis' is misrepresentative.

Progressive mechanical loading exercise—specifically eccentric training and heavy slow resistance (HSR) exercise—is the cornerstone of evidence-based tendinopathy management, stimulating tenocyte mechanotransduction, collagen synthesis, and structural remodeling.

Intratendinous corticosteroid injections should generally be avoided; while providing short-term pain relief, they impair long-term tenocyte proliferation, increase 1-year recurrence rates, and carry significant risks of tendon rupture.

Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT, radial or focused) provides effective non-invasive adjunct therapy for chronic recalcitrant tendinopathies (plantar fasciopathy, patellar, and calcific shoulder tendinopathy) by promoting local revascularization and tissue regeneration.

uncertainties: Efficacy and clinical reproducibility of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and autologous blood injections compared to sham saline in chronic tendinopathies.
Mechanisms and clinical indications for transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) targeting abnormal neo-vessels in refractory tendinopathy.
mcq_angles: Rationale for avoiding intratendinous corticosteroid injections (long-term structural weakening and elevated tendon rupture risk).
Principles of mechanotherapy: heavy slow resistance vs eccentric loading in stimulating tendon remodelation.

page.mentor_intro: Intravenous thrombolysis is the cornerstone of early medical reperfusion in acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Tenecteplase (TNK)—a genetically engineered bio-variant of alteplase (tissue plasminogen activator [tPA]) with greater fibrin specificity, longer half-life, and resistance to plasminogen activator inhibitor-1—allows single IV bolus administration. The landmark EXTEND-IA TNK randomized clinical trials established that tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg) achieves substantially higher early arterial reperfusion and superior functional recovery compared to alteplase prior to endovascular thrombectomy in patients with large vessel occlusion.

teaching_points.claim: Tenecteplase administered as a single intravenous bolus (0.25 mg/kg, maximum 25 mg over 5-10 seconds) demonstrated significantly higher substantial reperfusion (22% vs 10%, p = 0.004) and improved 90-day functional recovery compared to alteplase infusion in the EXTEND-IA TNK trial.

The single-bolus administration of tenecteplase streamlines emergency stroke workflow, eliminating the need for a 1-hour dedicated infusion pump and accelerating rapid inter-hospital transfer ('drip-and-ship') to comprehensive stroke centers for mechanical thrombectomy.

Tenecteplase demonstrates equivalent safety to alteplase regarding symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (sICH ~2-3%) and systemic bleeding when dosed at 0.25 mg/kg, whereas higher dosing (0.40 mg/kg, tested in EXTEND-IA TNK Part 2 and NOR-TEST 2) did not improve recanalization and increased haemorrhagic complications.

International stroke guidelines increasingly recommend tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as a preferred alternative to alteplase for acute ischaemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours, both in candidates for mechanical thrombectomy and in non-large vessel occlusion stroke.

uncertainties: Comparative efficacy of tenecteplase versus alteplase in minor, non-disabling acute ischaemic strokes (NIHSS 0-5) without large vessel occlusion.
Utility of tenecteplase in extended time windows (4.5 to 9 hours) or wake-up strokes guided by advanced automated perfusion mismatch imaging.
mcq_angles: Landmark findings of the EXTEND-IA TNK trial: tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg bolus doubled pre-thrombectomy angiographic recanalization compared to alteplase (0.9 mg/kg).
Optimal dosing of tenecteplase in acute stroke: why 0.25 mg/kg is the validated dose and why 0.40 mg/kg was abandoned due to excess bleeding without added efficacy.
Pharmacokinetic advantages of tenecteplase over alteplase (longer half-life permitting single IV bolus, 14-fold higher fibrin specificity, 80-fold greater resistance to PAI-1).

page.mentor_intro: Tension-type headache (TTH) is the most prevalent neurological primary headache disorder worldwide. Characterized by bilateral, non-pulsatile, pressing or tightening pain without migraine-associated features, management combines acute simple analgesics with prophylactic tricyclic antidepressants and behavioral lifestyle modifications.

teaching_points.claim: International Headache Society (ICHD-3) diagnostic criteria for tension-type headache require at least two of the following pain characteristics: bilateral location, pressing or tightening (non-pulsatile) quality, mild-to-moderate intensity, and not aggravated by routine physical activity (walking, climbing stairs).

TTH is strictly differentiated from migraine by the absence of severe nausea or vomiting and the presence of no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia; it is divided chronologically into episodic TTH (<15 days per month) and chronic TTH (>=15 days per month for >3 months).

First-line acute abortive therapy consists of simple analgesics: ibuprofen (400 mg), paracetamol (acetaminophen 1,000 mg), or naproxen (500 mg); acute medication use must be limited to <=2 days per week (or <10–15 days per month) to prevent the development of secondary medication overuse headache (MOH).

Amitriptyline (titrated from 10 mg at bedtime up to 25–75 mg daily) is the guideline-recommended first-line pharmacological prophylactic therapy for chronic and high-frequency episodic TTH, reducing headache frequency and duration by modulating central descending pain inhibition pathways; second-line alternatives include mirtazapine and venlafaxine.

Non-pharmacological and lifestyle interventions are foundational: stress management, biofeedback, cognitive behavioral therapy, acupuncture, physical therapy for pericranial muscle tenderness, regular sleep hygiene, and physical exercise all achieve significant reductions in headache frequency.

uncertainties: Efficacy of pericranial trigger point injections with local anesthetics or botulinum toxin in refractory chronic tension-type headache.
Comparative long-term adherence and efficacy of digital app-based mindfulness cognitive therapy versus daily tricyclic antidepressant prophylaxis.
mcq_angles: ICHD-3 differentiation from migraine: TTH is bilateral, pressing/tightening, not worsened by routine physical activity, and lacks nausea/vomiting.
First-line prophylactic pharmacotherapy for chronic TTH: low-dose amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant) taken at bedtime.
Medication overuse headache prevention: restrict acute analgesic intake to fewer than 10 to 15 days per month to avoid refractory secondary analgesic rebound headaches.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS, now classified as HRS-AKI) is a severe form of functional renal failure in advanced cirrhosis, driven by splanchnic arterial vasodilation, systemic arterial underfilling, and profound renal vasoconstriction. Terlipressin—a synthetic vasopressin V1a receptor agonist—induces potent splanchnic arterial vasoconstriction, redirecting blood volume to the systemic and renal circulations. The CONFIRM trial established terlipressin combined with intravenous albumin as the standard of care for reversing HRS-AKI; however, therapy carries significant risks of ischemic complications and respiratory failure from fluid overload, requiring baseline oxygenation and volume monitoring.

teaching_points.claim: Terlipressin combined with intravenous albumin (1 g/kg on day 1, followed by 20-40 g/day) is the first-line pharmacotherapy for HRS-AKI, achieving significantly higher rates of verified renal reversal compared to placebo or midodrine/octreotide (CONFIRM trial).

Continuous intravenous infusion of terlipressin (starting at 2 mg/day and titrating up to 12 mg/day) delivers equivalent renal reversal with significantly fewer ischemic and gastrointestinal adverse events compared to intermittent intravenous bolus dosing.

Respiratory failure is a major risk of terlipressin therapy; terlipressin is strictly contraindicated in patients with severe hypoxemia (SpO2 <90% on room air), acute pulmonary oedema, or active fluid overload, and patients must be screened for volume overload before initiating therapy.

Complete response to terlipressin is defined by a decrease in serum creatinine to <=1.5 mg/dL (or return to within 0.3 mg/dL of baseline); treatment is typically continued until creatinine reversal or for a maximum of 14 days.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term post-liver-transplantation survival among patients reversed with terlipressin versus norepinephrine infusions in the ICU.
Predictive role of novel urinary biomarkers (NGAL) in distinguishing acute tubular necrosis from pure functional HRS-AKI to predict terlipressin responsiveness.
mcq_angles: Recognizing major adverse effects and contraindications of terlipressin: respiratory failure/pulmonary oedema and peripheral ischemic necrosis.
Advantages of continuous IV terlipressin infusion over intermittent IV boluses in reducing adverse events while maintaining reversal rates.
Combining terlipressin with albumin (synergistic oncotic expansion and vasoconstriction) versus vasoconstrictor monotherapy.

page.mentor_intro: Chemotherapy for testicular germ cell tumours is guided by the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group (IGCCCG) risk classification, with bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP) remaining the standard frontline curative regimen. Good-risk disease is managed with 3 cycles of BEP or 4 cycles of EP (avoiding bleomycin pulmonary toxicity), while intermediate- and poor-risk disease requires 4 cycles of BEP. Surgical resection of residual masses post-chemotherapy is mandatory for NSGCT with lesions >1 cm to resect active teratoma or viable cancer, whereas pure seminoma residual masses <3 cm can be observed safely.

teaching_points.claim: First-line curative chemotherapy for metastatic TGCT utilizes BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin); good-risk disease achieves equivalent cure with 3 cycles of BEP or 4 cycles of EP to mitigate pulmonary fibrotic injury.

Bleomycin-induced pulmonary toxicity necessitates baseline and pre-cycle pulmonary function testing (DLCO); acute development of cough or dyspnoea warrants prompt cessation and high-dose corticosteroid therapy.

Residual retroperitoneal masses >1 cm post-chemotherapy in NSGCT require retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) due to high rates of mature teratoma (40%) or viable persistent carcinoma (10-15%).

Novel molecular biomarkers, particularly serum microRNA-371a-3p, demonstrate superior sensitivity and specificity compared to AFP/beta-hCG for detecting viable non-teratomatous residual tumour after chemotherapy.

uncertainties: Role of FDG-PET scanning in assessing post-chemotherapy residual lesions in NSGCT (ineffective for teratoma) versus its proven negative predictive value in seminoma.
Optimal salvage regimens (TIP: paclitaxel, ifosfamide, cisplatin vs high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell rescue) in first-line platinum-refractory relapse.
mcq_angles: Choice of regimen in good-risk metastatic germ cell tumours (3 cycles BEP vs 4 cycles EP) and recognizing bleomycin pulmonary toxicity criteria.
Management of post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal residual masses in NSGCT (mandatory RPLND if >1 cm) versus seminoma (observation if <3 cm, FDG-PET if >=3 cm).
Etoposide cumulative dosage thresholds and corresponding risks of therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukaemia.

page.mentor_intro: Testicular germ cell tumours (TGCTs) represent the most frequent solid malignancy in young men aged 15 to 35, divided fundamentally into seminomas and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (NSGCTs). Primary management hinges on initial radical inguinal orchiectomy with pre-operative serum tumour markers (alpha-fetoprotein [AFP], beta-hCG, and LDH), avoiding trans-scrotal biopsy to prevent lymphatic seeding. Long-term surveillance must balance cure rates exceeding 95% against late survivorship complications, including secondary cardiovascular disease and treatment-induced secondary leukaemias or solid malignancies.

teaching_points.claim: Radical inguinal orchiectomy with high ligation of the spermatic cord provides definitive histologic diagnosis and primary local control; trans-scrotal violation or percutaneous biopsy is strictly contraindicated due to disruption of normal lymphatic drainage.

Serum tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) must be measured prior to orchiectomy and tracked serially according to their half-lives (AFP 5-7 days; beta-hCG 24-36 hours); elevated AFP exclusively indicates non-seminomatous histology, as pure seminomas never produce AFP.

Gonadal function and sperm cryopreservation must be addressed prior to surgical orchiectomy and cytotoxic therapy, given high baseline rates of subfertility, oligospermia, and hypogonadism in TGCT patients.

Long-term survivorship monitoring is essential following platinum- and etoposide-based regimens, given cumulative risks of secondary acute myeloid leukaemias, metabolic syndrome, and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

uncertainties: Utility and clinical cutoff of circulating microRNAs (e.g., miR-371a-3p) compared to conventional serum markers for residual minimal disease detection.
Optimal surveillance intensity versus adjuvant single-agent carboplatin in stage I seminoma with adverse primary features (stromal invasion or rete testis involvement).
mcq_angles: Identifying pure seminoma versus NSGCT based on elevated serum AFP (pure seminoma cannot produce AFP; elevated AFP mandates management as NSGCT).
Initial surgical approach for a suspicious testicular mass (inguinal orchiectomy with high cord control vs contraindicated scrotal approach).
Long-term toxicity surveillance in TGCT survivors (cumulative etoposide-related secondary leukaemias and cisplatin-related vascular/renal toxicity).

page.mentor_intro: Thin Basement Membrane Nephropathy is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

Thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by heterozygous mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4, characterized by persistent microscopic hematuria with normal kidney function and minimal proteinuria; renal biopsy on electron microscopy shows uniform, diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane (<250 nm in adults) without the lamellation or podocyte foot-process effacement characteristic of Alport syndrome.

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are indicated in patients with thin basement membrane nephropathy who develop overt proteinuria (>0.5-1.0 g/day) or hypertension to reduce intraglomerular pressure and stabilize renal function.

page.mentor_intro: Third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerve palsies: pupil-sparing oculomotor palsy is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Botulinum Toxin Injection for the Treatment of Third, Fourth, and Sixth Nerve Palsy: A Meta-Analysis.

An acute isolated third cranial nerve (oculomotor) palsy with pupillary involvement (dilated, unreactive pupil) or partial pupillary involvement represents a neurological emergency mandating immediate CT angiography or catheter angiography to exclude an intracranial aneurysm (most commonly of the posterior communicating artery, PCoA); complete pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in patients with cardiovascular risk factors is typically caused by microvascular ischemia, which resolves spontaneously over 8-12 weeks.

Fourth cranial nerve (trochlear) palsy presents with vertical diplopia worsening on downgaze and head tilt toward the affected side, with patients adopting a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side (Bielschowsky head tilt test).

Sixth cranial nerve (abducens) palsy causes horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze towards the affected eye; in elderly patients, isolated abducens palsy is frequently microvascular, but in younger patients, elevated intracranial pressure or MS must be excluded.

uncertainties: Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerve palsies: pupil-sparing oculomotor palsy.
Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

page.mentor_intro: Point-of-care thoracic ultrasound (TUS) has transformed acute respiratory medicine and critical care, providing superior sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy over supine chest radiography for pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and consolidation. Standardized lung ultrasound evaluates sliding signs, horizontal A-lines (normal aeration), vertical B-lines (interstitial alveolar-interstitial syndrome), and consolidation with air bronchograms. Procedural thoracic ultrasound is the standard of care for pleural interventions, dramatically reducing iatrogenic pneumothorax, bleeding, and visceral laceration risks.

teaching_points.claim: Pleural sliding (shimmering movement of visceral and parietal pleura with respiration) paired with comet-tail artifacts definitively rules out pneumothorax at the interrogated intercostal space (negative predictive value ~100%).

The presence of multiple B-lines (laser-like vertical hyperechoic lines arising from the pleural line that move with sliding and erase A-lines) indicates increased interstitial water; >=3 B-lines per intercostal space denotes alveolar-interstitial syndrome (pulmonary oedema or pneumonitis).

Thoracic ultrasound differentiates transudative effusions (homogenously anechoic) from complex exudative effusions (septated, multi-loculated, with swirling debris or internal echogenicity), guiding thoracentesis vs chest tube fibrinolysis.

Dynamic ultrasound guidance or bedside pre-procedure mark-and-measure localization before pleural aspiration or drainage significantly reduces iatrogenic complications compared to blind percussion-guided techniques.

uncertainties: Utility and standardization of artificial intelligence automated algorithms for pleural volume quantification and effusion characterization.
Reliability of ultrasound in distinguishing cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from viral interstitial pneumonitis in acute exacerbations.
mcq_angles: Ultrasound signs excluding pneumothorax (lung sliding, B-lines, lung pulse) versus the diagnostic lung point establishing pneumothorax boundary.
Differentiating pulmonary oedema from acute respiratory distress syndrome based on B-line distribution (homogenous diffuse vs patchy with subpleural consolidations and pleural line irregularity).
Safety thresholds for thoracocentesis: identifying diaphragm position, spleen/liver margins, and minimum fluid depth (typically >=1.5-2 cm) throughout the respiratory cycle.
case_hooks: A 68-year-old woman in the ICU following central venous catheter insertion develops sudden tachypnoea; lung ultrasound demonstrates absence of lung sliding and barcode sign on M-mode.

A 55-year-old man with fever and left pleuritic pain has a pleural effusion on CXR; ultrasound shows extensive internal fibrinous septations ('honeycomb' appearance) indicating complex parapneumonic effusion.

page.mentor_intro: Mechanical endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) is the standard of care for acute ischaemic stroke caused by emergent large vessel occlusion (LVO) of the intracranial anterior circulation. Patient selection criteria have rapidly expanded from the historic 0-6 hour window (based on non-contrast CT ASPECTS >=6) to the extended 6-24 hour window. Extended-window selection (DAWN and DEFUSE-3 trials) relies on advanced CT/MRI perfusion imaging to demonstrate a clinical-core or target mismatch (small ischemic core with substantial salvageable ischemic penumbra and robust collateral circulation).

teaching_points.claim: Standard anterior circulation thrombectomy criteria within 0-6 hours include: pre-stroke mRS 0-1, causative occlusion of the internal carotid artery (ICA) or proximal middle cerebral artery (MCA-M1), age >=18 years, baseline NIHSS >=6, and non-contrast CT ASPECTS >=6.

Extended window thrombectomy (6-24 hours from last known well) requires physiological tissue imaging demonstrating salvageable penumbra: DAWN criteria (mismatch between clinical severity [NIHSS] and infarct core volume) or DEFUSE-3 criteria (ischemic core <70 mL, mismatch ratio >=1.8, and mismatch volume >=15 mL on CT perfusion or diffusion MRI).
Robust intracranial collateral circulation on multi-phase CTA predicts slower infarct core growth, lower hemorrhagic transformation rates, and improved functional independence post-recanalization.

Recent randomized clinical trials (RESCUE-Japan LIMIT, SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT) have established that EVT also benefits patients with large ischemic core infarcts (ASPECTS 3-5 or core >=50 mL), extending eligibility beyond conventional restricted criteria.

uncertainties: Efficacy and safety of mechanical thrombectomy in distal medium vessel occlusions (MeVOs: M2/M3 MCA, A2/A3 ACA, P2/P3 PCA).
Optimal post-thrombectomy blood pressure targets following complete TICI 2b/3 recanalization versus partial recanalization.
mcq_angles: Applying DAWN and DEFUSE-3 criteria for patient selection in the 6-24 hour extended window.
Calculating and interpreting the ASPECTS score on non-contrast CT (10-point scale evaluating 10 designated middle cerebral artery territory regions).
Expanding criteria: identifying the evidence supporting thrombectomy in large core infarctions (ASPECTS 3-5).

An 80-year-old male arrives 3 hours post-stroke onset with an NIHSS of 16; non-contrast head CT shows early ischemic changes in the insular ribbon and lentiform nucleus (ASPECTS = 8) with terminal ICA 'T' occlusion.

page.mentor_intro: Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <150 x 10^9/L) is a frequent haematologic abnormality resulting from decreased bone marrow production, increased peripheral destruction, splenic sequestration, or dilution. The initial clinical priority is excluding pseudothrombocytopenia (EDTA-dependent platelet clumping, ruled out by examining a peripheral blood smear and repeating the count in a citrated or heparinized tube). Urgent differentiation is required for life-threatening microangiopathic syndromes (TTP, HUS, DIC) and drug-induced etiologies (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia [HIT]), while distinguishing primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) from bone marrow failure.

teaching_points.claim: Pseudothrombocytopenia must always be ruled out by peripheral blood smear review showing platelet satellitism or clumping in EDTA; repeat analysis using a sodium citrate or heparin anticoagulant tube confirms the true platelet count.

A peripheral blood smear is mandatory in acute thrombocytopenia to evaluate for schistocytes (MAHA: TTP, HUS, DIC), blasts (acute leukaemia), dysplastic cells (myelodysplasia), or giant platelets (inherited thrombocytopenias or peripheral destruction).

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is a diagnosis of exclusion; frontline treatment for newly diagnosed active adult ITP with bleeding or platelets <20-30 x 10^9/L consists of oral corticosteroids (dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) with or without IVIG.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is evaluated via the 4Ts score (Thrombocytopenia magnitude, Timing of fall [days 5-10], Thrombosis, and absence of oTher causes); a high 4Ts score warrants immediate cessation of all heparin and initiation of a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, fondaparinux).

uncertainties: Predictive value of novel thrombopoietin receptor agonists (TPO-RAs: romiplostim, eltrombopag, avatrombopag) as upfront therapy alongside steroids in adult ITP.
Safety and efficacy of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) as alternatives to parenteral argatroban in acute HIT.
mcq_angles: Stepwise exclusion of pseudothrombocytopenia before invasive bone marrow testing.
Applying the 4Ts score in suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and selecting non-heparin anticoagulation.

Platelet transfusion thresholds: prophylactic threshold of 10 x 10^9/L in stable hypoproliferative patients, 20 x 10^9/L in febrile/septic patients, 50 x 10^9/L for major surgery, and 100 x 10^9/L for neurosurgery.
case_hooks: An asymptomatic 35-year-old male routine blood test shows a platelet count of 12 x 10^9/L; peripheral blood smear displays extensive large platelet aggregates in EDTA, which disperses in a citrated tube with normal count (220 x 10^9/L).
A 68-year-old post-cardiac surgery patient on enoxaparin prophylaxis experiences a 55% drop in platelets from 260 to 110 x 10^9/L on postoperative day 7, with new pain and swelling in his left calf.

page.mentor_intro: Renal thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) encompasses a spectrum of life-threatening disorders characterized by microvascular endothelial injury, platelet-rich microthrombi, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), consumptive thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury (AKI). Etiologies include atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS / complement-mediated TMA), Shiga toxin-producing E. coli HUS (STEC-HUS), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), calcineurin inhibitor toxicity, antibody-mediated allograft rejection, and malignant hypertension. Rapid differentiation is vital: while TTP requires immediate plasma exchange, complement-mediated TMA mandates early terminal complement blockade (eculizumab or ravulizumab) to salvage renal function.

teaching_points.claim: Renal TMA presents with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, negative Coombs test, elevated LDH, undetectable haptoglobin), profound or modest thrombocytopenia, and prominent acute kidney injury with proteinuria and haematuria.

Complement-mediated TMA (aHUS) results from genetic mutations or autoantibodies in regulatory complement proteins (Factor H, Factor I, MCP, C3); terminal C5 complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) achieve prompt haematologic remission and preserve long-term GFR if initiated early.

In kidney transplant recipients, TMA can be triggered de novo by calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), mTOR inhibitors, or acute antibody-mediated rejection (AMR); distinguishing drug toxicity from AMR requires C4d immunostaining and donor-specific antibody (DSA) testing.
Normal ADAMTS13 activity (>10-20%) excludes typical TTP and strongly supports complement-mediated TMA, secondary TMA, or STEC-HUS in patients with systemic microangiopathy and severe renal failure.

uncertainties: Duration of terminal complement inhibitor maintenance therapy (lifelong versus safe trial of discontinuation in genetically low-risk variants).
Role and diagnostic yield of complement gene testing panels in pregnancy-associated TMA versus pre-eclampsia/HELLP syndrome.
mcq_angles: Distinguishing aHUS from TTP based on degree of renal involvement (severe AKI vs predominantly neurological) and ADAMTS13 activity (>10% points towards aHUS).
Mechanisms and diagnostic evaluation of post-transplant TMA (calcineurin inhibitor arteriopathy vs acute antibody-mediated rejection with donor-specific antibodies).
Indications and timing for initiating C5 inhibitors (eculizumab/ravulizumab) in complement-mediated TMA with progressive azotemia.
case_hooks: A 34-year-old woman 2 weeks postpartum develops oliguria, BP 185/110 mmHg, platelet count 42 x 10^9/L, LDH 1450 U/L, schistocytes 3.8%, and creatinine 480 umol/L with ADAMTS13 activity of 65%.

A 52-year-old renal transplant recipient maintained on tacrolimus develops sudden allograft dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, and biopsy evidence of glomerular capillary thrombi and endothelial swelling.

page.mentor_intro: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) is a haematologic emergency caused by severe deficiency of the von Willebrand factor (VWF)-cleaving protease ADAMTS13 (<10% activity), leading to accumulation of ultra-large VWF multimers, platelet hyper-aggregation, and disseminated microvascular thrombosis. Acquired immune TTP (iTTP) is driven by anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies, whereas congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome) stems from biallelic ADAMTS13 gene mutations. The classic pentad (thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, neurological deficits, renal dysfunction, and fever) is rarely present simultaneously (<10%); unexplained MAHA and thrombocytopenia alone are sufficient to initiate immediate emergent therapeutic plasma exchange.

teaching_points.claim: TTP diagnosis is confirmed by severe ADAMTS13 activity deficiency (<10%); however, therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) must be initiated emergently upon clinical suspicion without waiting for laboratory assay results.

The PLASMIC score stratifies pre-test probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency based on platelet count <30, haemolysis markers, MCV <90 fL, INR <1.5, creatinine <2.0 mg/dL, and absence of active cancer or transplant.

Standard frontline therapy for immune TTP consists of the triple regimen: daily therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), high-dose corticosteroids, and caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody), with early rituximab (anti-CD20) to deplete autoantibody-producing B cells.
Platelet transfusions are contraindicated in suspected TTP unless life-threatening haemorrhage occurs, as they can accelerate microvascular thrombosis and precipitate acute clinical deterioration.

uncertainties: Optimal timing and monitoring for caplacizumab discontinuation guided by ADAMTS13 activity recovery (>20%).
Role of upfront recombinant ADAMTS13 enzyme replacement therapy versus plasma exchange in acquired immune TTP compared to congenital TTP.
mcq_angles: Applying the PLASMIC score to guide immediate empiric plasma exchange while ADAMTS13 results are pending.
Mechanism of action of caplacizumab (binds A1 domain of VWF, preventing platelet GPIb-IX-V interaction) and its impact on time to platelet normalization and prevention of exacerbations.
Contraindication to prophylactic platelet transfusion in TTP versus other thrombocytopenic disorders.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old woman presents to the ED with confusion, petechiae, platelet count 14 x 10^9/L, Hb 7.8 g/dL, LDH 1890 U/L, peripheral schistocytes 4%, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL.
A 45-year-old man with confirmed iTTP experiences a drop in platelets from 180 to 45 x 10^9/L three days after completing a 5-day course of TPE while off caplacizumab.

page.mentor_intro: Modern management of immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP) has evolved from plasma exchange and steroids alone to quadruple-target therapy incorporating caplacizumab and rituximab. Caplacizumab, a bivalent anti-vWF nanobody targeting the A1 domain, rapidly inhibits platelet adhesion to ultra-large vWF multimers, halting microvascular thrombosis within hours. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) removes circulating ultra-large vWF multimers and neutralizing anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies while replenishing functional ADAMTS13 enzyme until endogenous production recovers.

teaching_points.claim: Caplacizumab administered as an initial IV loading dose followed by daily subcutaneous dosing significantly shortens time to platelet count normalization and drastically reduces TTP-related mortality and refractory disease.

Therapeutic plasma exchange (1.0 to 1.5 plasma volume exchange with fresh frozen plasma) must be continued daily until the platelet count is maintained >=150 x 10^9/L for at least 2 consecutive days, alongside LDH normalization.
Caplacizumab must be continued throughout the duration of daily plasma exchange and for 30 days following the cessation of TPE, with extension if ADAMTS13 activity remains suppressed (<20%).

Adverse bleeding events, primarily mucocutaneous (epistaxis, gingival bleeding) and menorrhagia, are common with caplacizumab; holding caplacizumab is indicated prior to major invasive procedures or in active severe bleeding.

uncertainties: Utility of recombinant ADAMTS13 as an adjunctive or standalone agent to minimize or eliminate the need for plasma exchange.
Cost-effectiveness and optimal biomarker-guided cessation protocols for caplacizumab in resource-constrained health systems.
mcq_angles: Criteria for terminating daily therapeutic plasma exchange (platelets >=150 for 2 days + LDH normalization) versus duration of post-TPE caplacizumab maintenance.
Managing caplacizumab during bleeding episodes or elective invasive procedures (temporary interruption and monitoring vWF ristocetin cofactor activity).
Role of concurrent rituximab in suppressing anti-ADAMTS13 IgG antibodies and reducing 1-year relapse rates in acquired iTTP.
case_hooks: A 36-year-old female with acute iTTP achieves platelet normalization on day 3 of TPE plus caplacizumab; on day 5 after stopping TPE, ADAMTS13 activity remains at 4%, prompting decision on caplacizumab continuation.
A patient receiving caplacizumab for iTTP develops significant gingival bleeding and epistaxis with normal platelets, requiring assessment of anti-vWF pharmacodynamics.

page.mentor_intro: Thymic epithelial tumours (TETs)—comprising thymomas and thymic carcinomas—are the most prevalent anterior mediastinal neoplasms in adults. Thymomas are uniquely linked with autoimmune paraneoplastic syndromes, most prominently myasthenia gravis (observed in 30-50% of thymoma cases), pure red cell aplasia, and Good syndrome (hypogammaglobulinaemia). Complete surgical resection (R0) with en bloc thymectomy remains the single most critical prognostic determinant, utilizing Masaoka-Koga or the 8th/9th edition IASLC/ITMIG TNM staging systems.

teaching_points.claim: Complete en bloc surgical resection (thymectomy with complete mediastinal adipose clearance) is the cornerstone of curative therapy for early and resectable thymic epithelial tumours; R0 margin status dictates long-term overall survival.

Myasthenia gravis screening (acetylcholine receptor autoantibody testing) is mandatory in all patients presenting with an anterior mediastinal mass, even in the absence of overt neuromuscular symptoms, to avoid post-operative myasthenic crisis.

Masaoka-Koga clinical staging differentiates Stage I (completely encapsulated), Stage II (microscopic or macroscopic capsular/mediastinal fat invasion), Stage III (invasion of neighboring organs like pericardium, great vessels, lung), and Stage IV (pleural/pericardial dissemination or distant metastases).

Minimally invasive thymectomy (video-assisted thoracic surgery [VATS] or robot-assisted thoracic surgery [RATS]) provides equivalent oncologic margins with reduced blood loss and shorter hospital stays compared to open sternotomy in early-stage (I-II) tumours.

uncertainties: Role of neoadjuvant chemotherapy or immunotherapy in locally advanced unresectable Masaoka Stage III/IV thymic carcinoma.
Utility of baseline 18F-FDG PET SUVmax cutoffs in predicting progression-free survival and distinguishing low-risk from high-risk histology.
mcq_angles: Differentiating thymoma from thymic carcinoma on histology and immunohistochemistry (CD5, CD117/KIT positivity strongly favors thymic carcinoma; aggressive clinical behaviour with early lymph node and hematogenous metastases).

Preoperative preparation of a thymoma patient with concurrent myasthenia gravis (optimizing anticholinesterase/immunosuppressive therapy, IVIG/plasma exchange to prevent post-extubation respiratory failure).
Indications for adjuvant radiotherapy following thymectomy (beneficial in Masaoka Stage II with positive/close margins and Stage III completely resected tumours).

page.mentor_intro: Thyroid carcinoma represents the most common endocrine malignancy, predominantly comprising differentiated thyroid cancers (DTC: papillary 85%, follicular 10%), alongside medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC, derived from parafollicular C-cells), and highly lethal anaplastic carcinoma. Risk stratification (ATA guidelines) drives personalized surgical extent—ranging from active surveillance for selected low-risk microcarcinomas (<1 cm) and thyroid lobectomy, to total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection. Postoperative radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation is reserved for intermediate-to-high risk DTC, while TSH suppression therapy is calibrated to recurrence risk.

teaching_points.claim: Initial risk stratification by American Thyroid Association (ATA) criteria categorizes DTC into low, intermediate, and high risk of recurrence, determining the necessity for total thyroidectomy versus unilateral lobectomy.

Radioactive iodine (RAI, 131-I) remnant ablation is not routinely recommended for ATA low-risk patients (<1 cm unifocal or up to 4 cm intrathyroidal papillary carcinomas without nodal metastases), reducing unnecessary radiation exposure.

Post-thyroidectomy surveillance relies on stimulated or unsuppressed serum thyroglobulin (Tg) paired with anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) and high-resolution neck ultrasonography; rising TgAb titers can falsely depress measured Tg and indicate recurrence.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma requires testing for germline RET proto-oncogene mutations (MEN2A/2B syndromes) and screening for pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines) prior to surgical neck exploration.

uncertainties: Optimal role of active surveillance versus immediate surgical resection in low-risk microcarcinomas (<1 cm) in younger cohorts.
Efficacy of redifferentiation therapy with MAPK/BRAF inhibitors prior to RAI in radioactive iodine-refractory metastatic DTC.
mcq_angles: Selecting thyroid lobectomy vs total thyroidectomy in differentiated thyroid cancer based on tumour size (1-4 cm), extrathyroidal extension, and nodal status.

Interpretation of thyroglobulin (Tg) in the presence of positive anti-Tg antibodies (anti-Tg antibodies cause falsely low Tg on immunometric assays; trending antibody titers serves as a surrogate tumour marker).
Preoperative mandatory workup in suspected medullary thyroid cancer (calcitonin, CEA, germline RET testing, and ruling out bilateral pheochromocytoma).

A 48-year-old man post-total thyroidectomy for follicular thyroid cancer has an undetectable serum Tg (<0.1 ng/mL) but anti-Tg antibodies have doubled over 6 months from 50 to 110 IU/mL.

page.mentor_intro: Long-term surveillance for differentiated thyroid carcinoma (papillary and follicular) utilizes high-resolution cervical ultrasonography and serial serum thyroglobulin measurements. Risk-stratified follow-up allows tailoring of TSH suppression therapy and avoids unnecessary invasive imaging in patients achieving an excellent response to treatment.

teaching_points.claim: Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) measured alongside anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) is the primary sensitive tumor marker for recurrent differentiated thyroid carcinoma following total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation; any presence of TgAb invalidates automated immunometric Tg assays and mandates radioimmunoassay or LC-MS/MS measurement.

High-resolution neck ultrasonography performed at 6 to 12 months post-ablation and periodically thereafter evaluates the central and lateral cervical nodal basins; suspicious features include microcalcifications, round shape, cystic necrosis, hyperechoic punctate foci, and loss of the fatty hilum.

According to the American Thyroid Association (ATA) dynamic risk stratification, patients are reclassified into excellent response, biochemically incomplete response, structurally incomplete response, or indeterminate response based on follow-up imaging and stimulated/unstimulated Tg levels.

In patients achieving an 'excellent response' (undetectable unstimulated Tg <0.2 ng/mL or stimulated Tg <1 ng/mL with negative imaging), TSH targets are relaxed to the normal reference range (0.5-2.0 mIU/L), minimizing iatrogenic risks of osteoporosis and atrial fibrillation.

uncertainties: Optimal interval for routine ultrasound surveillance in low-risk patients who maintain undetectable thyroglobulin beyond 5 years.
Clinical threshold for empiric radioiodine therapy versus surveillance in patients with biochemically incomplete response without structural localization.
mcq_angles: Laboratory pitfall with thyroglobulin: anti-Tg antibodies falsely lower immunometric Tg measurements; serial monitoring must always include concurrent TgAb titers.
Lymph node biopsy threshold: suspicious cervical lymph nodes should undergo ultrasound-guided FNA with needle washout for Tg measurement when measuring >=8-10 mm in smallest diameter.
TSH suppression targets: maintain TSH <0.1 mIU/L for high-risk persistent disease, 0.1-0.5 mIU/L for intermediate risk, and 0.5-2.0 mIU/L for low-risk complete responders.
case_hooks: A 46-year-old woman 1 year post-total thyroidectomy and 131-I ablation whose serum Tg is undetectable (<0.1 ng/mL) but anti-Tg antibody rises from 15 to 140 IU/mL.
A 55-year-old man with treated papillary thyroid cancer whose routine surveillance ultrasound detects a 12-mm round, hypoechoic lymph node in level IV with microcalcifications.

page.mentor_intro: Thyroid disease spans disorders of hormone synthesis and function (hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) and structural pathology (goitre, thyroiditis, benign nodules, and thyroid malignancies). Third-generation serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) serves as the primary, most sensitive screening test, with reflexive free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) determining overt versus subclinical disease. Etiologic evaluation utilizes thyroid autoantibodies (anti-TPO and anti-Tg for Hashimoto thyroiditis; TSH receptor antibodies [TRAb/TSI] for Graves' disease) and radioactive iodine uptake/scintigraphy to guide targeted antithyroid medications, radioiodine ablation, or surgery.

teaching_points.claim: Serum TSH is the single most sensitive first-line test for evaluating thyroid functional status due to the logarithmic inverse relationship between TSH and circulating free thyroid hormones.

Subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal free T4) carries risks of progression to overt failure, dyslipidemia, and adverse pregnancy outcomes; levothyroxine treatment is strongly indicated for TSH >=10 mIU/L, during pregnancy, or in symptomatic younger individuals with positive anti-TPO antibodies.

Graves' disease is distinguished from destructive thyroiditis (subacute, painless, or postpartum thyroiditis) by positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) and diffuse high uptake on radioactive iodine scanning, whereas destructive thyroiditis exhibits low or absent uptake.

Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is categorized into Type 1 (iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in underlying latent thyroid autonomy, treated with thionamides) and Type 2 (destructive thyroiditis in normal glands, treated with systemic corticosteroids); differentiating via color flow Doppler ultrasound is essential.

uncertainties: Cardiovascular risk-benefit balance of treating subclinical hyperthyroidism (TSH <0.1 mIU/L) in asymptomatic individuals aged <65 years.
Optimal timing and thresholds for radioiodine versus long-term low-dose thionamide maintenance in relapsed Graves' disease.
mcq_angles: Differentiating Graves' disease from subacute thyroiditis based on radioactive iodine uptake (high/diffuse vs suppressed/absent) and vascularity on Doppler ultrasound.
Treatment thresholds for subclinical hypothyroidism: universally treating when TSH >=10 mIU/L or during pregnancy/conception.
Managing amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis: distinguishing Type 1 (thionamides + potassium perchlorate) from Type 2 (corticosteroids).

A 42-year-old female presents with neck tenderness, fever, palpitations, and an elevated ESR of 85 mm/h following a viral upper respiratory infection; radioactive iodine uptake is <1%.

teaching_points.claim: Clinical practice guideline consensus establishes evidence-directed diagnostic criteria and risk-stratified therapy for thyroiditis: hashimotos, de quervains, postpartum - phases, tsh trajectory, management: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice and Multi-Society Consensus on Thyroiditis: Hashimotos, de Quervains, postpartum - phases, TSH trajectory, management.

Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) and postpartum thyroiditis classically follow a triphasic clinical and biochemical trajectory: an initial thyrotoxic phase (caused by follicular disruption and release of preformed hormone, characterized by low radioiodine/technetium uptake) lasting 2-8 weeks, followed by a transient hypothyroid phase, and eventual euthyroid recovery in >90% of cases; thyrotoxic symptoms are treated with beta-blockers rather than antithyroid drugs (which are ineffective).

Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterized by elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies leading to chronic autoimmune destruction and permanent hypothyroidism requiring lifelong levothyroxine.

Subacute de Quervain thyroiditis typically presents with severe anterior neck pain radiating to the jaw, markedly elevated ESR/CRP, and rapid relief following nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or oral corticosteroids.

page.mentor_intro: Thyroid nodules are exceptionally common, detected in up to 50-60% of healthy adults on high-resolution ultrasonography, but fewer than 5-10% harbor malignancy. The initial evaluation mandates serum TSH measurement: a suppressed TSH warrants radionuclide scintigraphy (hot/hyperfunctioning nodules rarely represent malignancy and do not require biopsy). Euthyroid or hypothyroid nodules are risk-stratified using standardized ultrasound systems (ACR TI-RADS or EU-TIRADS), which dictate the size thresholds for fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy classified by the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology.

teaching_points.claim: Initial laboratory evaluation of a thyroid nodule must begin with serum TSH; if TSH is subnormal, a radionuclide thyroid scan (technetium-99m or I-123) should be performed to detect autonomous hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodules, which are rarely malignant and do not require FNA.

Ultrasound features conferring high risk of malignancy include: solid composition, hypoechogenicity, taller-than-wide shape, irregular/infiltrative margins, and punctate echogenic foci (microcalcifications).

According to ACR TI-RADS, FNA thresholds are based on cumulative feature points: TR3 (mildly suspicious) FNA at >=2.5 cm; TR4 (moderately suspicious) FNA at >=1.5 cm; and TR5 (highly suspicious) FNA at >=1.0 cm, safely reducing unnecessary biopsies of benign nodules.

The Bethesda System categorizes FNA cytology into six tiers (I: Non-diagnostic; II: Benign; III: AUS/FLUS; IV: Follicular neoplasm; V: Suspicious for malignancy; VI: Malignant); molecular testing (e.g., Afirma, ThyroSeq) is indicated for indeterminate categories (Bethesda III and IV) to rule in or rule out malignancy.

uncertainties: Role of contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) and shear-wave elastography as adjuncts to refine FNA selection in indeterminate nodules.
Cost-effectiveness and long-term diagnostic accuracy of next-generation sequencing molecular panels in diverse non-Caucasian populations.
mcq_angles: Applying ACR TI-RADS points and size thresholds for recommending FNA versus ultrasound surveillance.
Management of Bethesda Category III (AUS/FLUS) and IV (Follicular neoplasm): utilizing molecular diagnostic testing or repeat FNA versus immediate diagnostic lobectomy.
Recognizing benign ultrasound patterns (purely cystic nodules or spongiform nodules >50%) that do not require biopsy.
